Bestiary
(Swarm) A swarm is a group of smaller creatures. It
covers all surfaces in its space. If it has the flier trait, it
fills its space. When moving, the swarm can move freely
through openings large enough to permit the passage
of a single member and through the spaces of other
creatures. Other creatures can enter the swarm’s space
and move through it. The swarm’s space counts as
difficult terrain.
		 A swarm takes half damage from effects that use an
attack roll and double damage from effects that require
it to make a challenge roll.
Undead Undead are not alive. An undead creature
is never affected by deprivation or exposure and
ignores any effect that would age it. When it becomes
incapacitated, the animating force dissipates, leaving
behind dead remains.
		 Some undead creatures are nearly mindless and are
immune to many afflictions that affect thought and
awareness. Intelligent, self-directed undead are more
susceptible to such effects.
Characteristics
and Attributes
The next few lines present numbers representing the
creature’s characteristics and attributes.
Perception: This entry tells you the creature’s Perception
score and modifier.
Special Senses: If a creature has a special sense, it is
noted here. Rules for the most common types of senses
follow. Special senses beyond these are described in full in
the creature’s entry.
Shadowsight The creature can see in areas obscured by
shadows as if those areas were lit.
Darksight The creature can see in areas obscured by
shadows and darkness within medium range of it as if
those areas were lit. Beyond this distance, the creature
treats darkness as shadows and shadows as lit.
Sightless The creature relies on senses other than
sight to perceive its surroundings and can pinpoint the
location of each creature and object within long range
of it. Creatures within the area cannot hide from the
creature, and it ignores banes imposed by obscurement
on rolls to perceive things. A sightless creature is never
subject to the blinded affliction.
Truesight The creature can see in areas obscured by
shadows and darkness as if those areas were lit. The
creature can also see invisible creatures and objects, and it
automatically recognizes illusions it sees for what they are.
Defense: This entry tells you the creature’s Defense
score. A creature’s Defense score might be higher than its
Agility, due to natural armor or intrinsic abilities. Creatures
that wear armor or use shields note them parenthetically
after the score.
Health: The creature’s Health score. When a creature
that is not a player character becomes incapacitated, it dies
instantly unless you decide otherwise.
Attributes: The scores and modifiers for the creature’s
four attributes are listed here. If an attribute entry has a
“—” instead of a number, the creature does not have that
attribute and is immune to anything that would target that
attribute or require a roll using it.
Speed: The creature’s Speed, measured in yards. If the
creature has any special movement traits, they are noted
here. If a special movement entry includes a number, the
creature uses that number in place of its normal Speed
when moving in this way. See Special Forms of Movement
in Chapter 2 for more information.
Climber The creature ignores difficult terrain from
climbing.
Flier The creature can move by flying.
(Swoop) While flying, the creature’s movement never
triggers free attacks.
Swimmer The creature ignores difficult terrain from
swimming.
Immune: If the creature is unaffected by certain damage
sources or afflictions, they are listed here. Otherwise, this
line is absent.
Defensive Trait: If the creature has any special defenses,
they are described here. Otherwise, this line is absent.
Vulnerability: If the creature gains afflictions from or is
otherwise harmed by certain environments or situations,
they are described here. Otherwise, this line is absent.
Other Trait or Passive Talent: If the creature has any
other special trait or a talent that doesn’t require it to take
an action, it is noted here. Otherwise, this line is absent.
Insanity and Corruption
The Insanity and Corruption scores shown for creatures in
this chapter represent typical values. You can increase or
decrease these numbers as you see fit.
Attack Options
When the creature uses an action to attack, it may choose
from any of the listed options. Unless otherwise noted, the
creature attacks one target creature or object and makes its
attack roll against the target’s Defense.
(Reach +#): Most creatures have a reach of 1 or their Size,
whichever is larger. If a creature has a longer reach, that is
noted here.
(Range): Ranged attacks note the range (short, medium,
long, or extreme).
Natural Weapon: Natural weapons can be anything
a creature uses to hunt or to protect itself, such as teeth,
claws, spines, horns, or a tail spike.
Attack Talents
This entry describes any additional effects on the target
from a success on the attack roll using this talent. Certain
attack talents take effect only if the creature gets a success

---

Bestiary
on an attack roll total of 20 or higher and exceeds the
target’s Defense by 5 or more. This is written in abbreviated
form as “on attack roll 20+” on the attack line.
Special Attacks
Some creatures have talents that grant them special attacks,
which are described in this entry. Using a special attack
counts as an attack action. If the creature has no special
attacks, this entry is absent.
Multiple Attacks: Many creatures can make two or more
attacks using a single attack action. For example, a creature
with Double Attack can use one action to make two attack
rolls. Unless otherwise noted, these attacks can be against
the same target or different ones.
Special Actions
Some creatures can use special actions, which are
described in this entry. Taking a special action uses an
action unless otherwise specified. If the creature has no
special actions, this entry is absent.
Magic
This category is present only if the creature knows any spells.
Power: The creature’s Power score.
Tradition and Spells: The spells the creature knows are
organized alphabetically by tradition. Each tradition is set
out on a separate line. Each spell includes the number of
castings available for that spell (in parentheses).
End of the Round
This entry describes anything that happens at the end of
the round if the creature is not incapacitated. When combat
starts, you resolve any such effects as though a previous
round had ended and then proceed with the first round.
Creature
Descriptions
This chapter presents creatures in alphabetical order,
followed by entries for typical characters who might be
encountered. For an index of all the creatures in the game,
presented in order of Difficulty, see the end of this chapter.
Amphisbaena
From the deserts of the Desolation to the dungeons of
powerful wizards, amphisbaenas infest places rich in
magical energies. Amphisbaenas grow up to 12 feet long
and have two heads, one at each end of their bodies. Their
coloration varies based on their environment, such that
those dwelling in the Desolation have red and brown
scales, subterranean breeds have black scales, while arctic-
dwelling amphisbaenas are white and blue. Regardless of
their coloration, all amphisbaenas have emerald eyes that
gleam in the dark.
AMPHISBAENA DIFFICULTY 25
Size 2 monster
Perception 14 (+4); darksight
Defense 16; Health 30; Insanity —; Corruption 0
Strength 13 (+3), Agility 15 (+5), Intellect 8 (–2), Will 11 (+1)
Speed 12
Immune damage from cold; dazed, impaired, stunned
Two Heads An amphisbaena can take both a fast turn and a
slow turn and can use two triggered actions each round.
ATTACK OPTIONS
Fangs (melee) +5 (1d6 + 1 plus Poison)
Poison The target must make a Strength challenge roll with
1 bane. On a failure, it takes 1d6 damage and becomes
poisoned for 1 minute. If it is already poisoned, the target
instead takes 1d6 extra damage.
SPECIAL ACTIONS
Pinning Gaze The amphisbaena uses a triggered action
on its turn to fix its gaze on one target creature within
medium range of it. The target must make a Will

challenge roll. On a failure, it becomes immobilized until
it uses an action to remove the affliction. On a success,
it becomes immune to that amphisbaena’s Pinning Gaze
until the target completes a rest.
Animal
Animals come in a variety of sizes and environments. They
might be ordinary beasts or gigantic versions of mundane
animals. You can customize animals quickly by adding
traits and talents.

Bestiary
Animal swarms comprise groups of bats, rats, frogs,
sparrows, or any other tiny animal. In large numbers, even
normally harmless creatures can be dangerous. Add the
flier trait to create flocks of flying creatures and the aquatic
trait to create schools of piranha.
Animated Corpse
The remains of once-living creatures now infused by dark
magic, animated corpses make obedient servants that shuffle
where directed without concern for themselves. Animated
corpses appear in whatever state their makers found them,
ranging from little more than clattering bones held together
with leather straps to fully intact corpses that could pass for
living if not for their deathly pallor and lack of response.

Speed 6

Barghest
Barghests race out from Hell’s gates to hunt down and
destroy those damned souls whose time is up. Resembling
great hounds with coal black coats, fiery red eyes, and curls
of sulfurous smoke rising from their bodies, they evoke
dread in all who look upon them.
BARGHEST DIFFICULTY 250
Size 2 horrifying faerie (devil)
Perception 20 (+10); truesight
Defense 17; Health 70; Insanity —; Corruption 0
Strength 15 (+5), Agility 14 (+4), Intellect 10 (+0), Will 15 (+5)
Speed 14
Immune damage from cold or fire; charmed, compelled,
frightened
Resilience A barghest takes half damage from weapons.
Spell Defense A barghest takes half damage from spells
and makes any challenge roll to resist a spell with 1 boon.
A creature attacking the barghest with a spell makes the
attack roll with 1 bane.
Consumed by Hellfire When a barghest becomes
incapacitated, hellfire fills a 10-yard-radius sphere
centered on a point within its space, consuming its body.
Each creature in the area must make an Agility challenge
roll with 2 banes, taking 5d6 + 10 damage on a failure or
half the damage on a success.
Life Sense A barghest knows the location of each living
creature within 1 mile of it. Such creatures cannot
become hidden from the barghest, and the barghest’s
attack rolls ignore banes imposed by obscurement
against living targets.
Iron Vulnerability A barghest is impaired while it is in
contact with iron.
ATTACK OPTIONS
Teeth (melee) +5 with 3 boons (4d6 plus 2d6 from fire)
SPECIAL ATTACKS
Hell Awaits The barghest uses an action, or a triggered
action on its turn, to make a Will attack roll against the
Will of one creature within medium range that can see
it. The barghest makes the attack roll with 3 boons if
the target has any Corruption. On a success, the target
gains 1 Insanity and becomes cursed (as a rank 5 spell)
for 1 hour or until the barghest becomes incapacitated.
Until the curse is lifted, the target cannot heal damage
and is impaired. A creature cursed by the barghest dies
instantly when it becomes incapacitated, and Hell claims
its soul. The creature cannot be restored to life by magic.
		 Once the barghest uses Hell Awaits, it cannot do so
again for 1 minute.
SPECIAL ACTIONS
Fires of Hell When a creature within the barghest’s reach
deals damage to it, the barghest can use a triggered
action to spew flames from its mouth. The triggering
creature must get a success on an Agility challenge roll
or take 2d6 damage.
Hound of Hell When a creature moves out of the
barghest’s reach, the barghest can use a triggered action
to move up to its Speed toward the triggering creature.
This movement does not trigger free attacks.
END OF THE ROUND
Burned by Sunlight The barghest takes 2d6 damage if it is
in an area lit by sunlight.

Bestiary
Barrow Wight
Barrow wights rise from the remains of great warriors and
chieftains, men and women noted for their courage and
skill in battle. Devotion to their people, anger over a wrong
done, or a vile curse placed on them by their enemies
prevents them from finding the peace of oblivion promised
by the Underworld. And so they wait in their graves, their
souls trapped inside their moldering bodies, for the time
when their people need them again.
Barrow wights look like emaciated humans, skin drawn
taught over the bones, eyes replaced by pools of darkness
in which float pinpricks of blue light. Most wear the armor
they wore in life, and some still wield whatever weapons
they were interred with. They retain the ability to speak,
usually in ancient languages such as High Archaic, in quiet,
whispering voices.
BARROW WIGHT DIFFICULTY 25
Size 1 horrifying undead
Perception 13 (+3); darksight
Defense 15 (mail); Health 35; Insanity —; Corruption 2
Strength 13 (+3), Agility 11 (+1), Intellect 10 (+0), Will 13 (+3)
Speed 10
Immune damage from cold, disease, or poison; asleep,
diseased, fatigued, poisoned
Sunlight Vulnerability A barrow wight is impaired while in
an area lit by sunlight.
ATTACK OPTIONS
Claws (melee) +3 with 3 boons (2d6 plus Life Drain)
Life Drain If living, the target must make a Strength
challenge roll with 1 bane. On a failure, the target
becomes impaired for 1 minute. When a creature
impaired in this way becomes incapacitated, it dies
instantly and rises as a compelled animated corpse 1d6
rounds later.
Basilisk
A magnificent serpent of incredible size, a basilisk is
covered with glittering black scales from its wide, flat
head to its tapering tail. Its maw sports four fangs, each
as long as a scimitar and dripping with steaming poison.
The basilisk’s most notable features, however, are its
golden gleaming eyes. Few survive looking into their
dreadful gaze.
Basilisks make their lairs in sinkholes, caves, and old
ruins, where their noxious presence sickens the land and
drives off or kills living things. The longer the monster
remains, the greater the blight, until the ground around
its lair is strewn with brittle bones and blackened,
skeletal trees.
Basilisks prefer to live alone, gathering in numbers only
to mate. Powerful magicians and dark priests sometimes
compel basilisks to serve as guardians for ancient and
powerful treasures, or to protect entrances into their lairs.
BASILISK DIFFICULTY 250
Size 3 monster
Perception 12 (+2); darksight
Defense 18; Health 100; Insanity 0; Corruption 1
Strength 17 (+7), Agility 11 (+1), Intellect 8 (–2), Will 11 (+1)
Speed 12
Captivating Appearance On first seeing a basilisk, a creature
must make a Will challenge roll with 3 banes. On a failure,
the creature gains 1 Insanity and cannot avert its eyes from
the basilisk for 1 round. Whether it gets a success or failure,
it is immune to that basilisk’s Captivating Appearance until
after that creature completes a rest.
ATTACK OPTIONS
Fangs (melee) +7 with 3 boons (4d6 plus Poison)
Poison The target must make a Strength challenge roll with
3 banes. It takes 4d6 damage and becomes poisoned for
1 minute on a failure, or just takes half the damage on a
success. If the target is already poisoned, it instead takes
4d6 extra damage.
		 At the end of each round, a creature poisoned in this
way must make a Strength challenge roll. On a failure, it
takes 2d6 damage and also becomes dazed for 1 round.
END OF THE ROUND
Killing Gaze Each creature within medium range of the
basilisk that can see it must either use a triggered action
to avert its eyes from the basilisk’s gaze or make a
Strength challenge roll with 2 banes.
		 For 1 round, a creature that averted its eyes makes
attack rolls with 2 banes and other creatures make
attack rolls against it with 2 boons.
		 A creature that gets a failure on the Strength
challenge roll takes 3d6 damage. A creature that
becomes incapacitated by this damage dies instantly.
Bear
This entry describes especially large bears, such as grizzly
and polar bears, which are more dangerous than other
animals of their size. Ogres sometimes keep bears as pets.
BEAR DIFFICULTY 50
Size 2 animal
Perception 12 (+2); shadowsight
Defense 14; Health 55; Insanity 0; Corruption 0
Strength 16 (+6), Agility 10 (+0), Intellect 7 (–3), Will 9 (–1)
Speed 12

Bestiary
Beastman
These primitive and brutal beings fuse animalistic
characteristics with humanoid forms. Beastmen are
usually fur-covered and have the heads of beasts, such
as goats, wolves, bears, rats, bulls, and others. They
wield simple weapons and strap crude armor on their
bodies, often adorning their equipment with symbols
of the demon prince honored by their particular tribe.
Filth and dried blood cling to them, crusting on seeping
wounds from battles fought with their age-old enemies
or each other.
According to legend, the beastmen rejected the gods of
the Old Faith in a long-past age. For their blasphemies, the
gods took from them the gift of the human form, rendering
them little better than animals. The curse plunged the
beastmen into madness and evil, impelling them to pledge
service to the demons of the Void and do the dark work of
the Demon Lord.
Beastmen gather in wild places: deep forests, empty plains,
and abandoned, ruined cities, where they raise profane
altars. Their bizarre rituals involve cutting into their flesh,
rutting with each other, killing and eating, and mad raving.
Their hoots and barks form an unholy chorus that carries for
miles around. As the tribes grow larger, shamans emerge to
direct the hordes against human settlements to plunder, take
slaves, or simply vent their ever-present bloodlust.
FOMOR DIFFICULTY 1
Size 1 beastman
Perception 10 (+0); shadowsight
Defense 14 (soft leather, small shield); Health 10; Insanity 3;
Corruption 2
Strength 10 (+0), Agility 12 (+2), Intellect 8 (–2), Will 7 (–3)
Speed 10
Craven A fomor is frightened while within the reach of two
or more creatures that are hostile to it.
ATTACK OPTIONS

them ahead to flush out prey for the wargs to pick off one at
a time.
A warg has a human body covered in patchy brown, gray,
or white fur that grows thicker toward its wolf-like head.
When one moves, it alternates between walking on its
legs and running on all fours. Wargs steal gear from their
victims but rarely care for it, so their weapons are rusty and
notched and their armor is falling apart.

suffering, their oozing bodies stripped of skin and forced

tangled claws.

hills and mountains, hooting and barking as they give
chase to prey and copulate with it before devouring what’s
left from their disturbing sport. They cannot be reasoned
with and are a serious threat to anyone living near their
hunting grounds.

shoulders. Instead, a crude face leers from the center of its
body, its wide, slobbery maw filled with shovel-like teeth
and uttering all manner of strange and unholy sounds.
When a boggart bothers to speak, it does so in a brutish,
rumbling tongue, spraying its audience with stinking spittle
and punctuating what passes for words with belches and
mad laughter.

Broodling
For as long as humans have existed, there have been
broodlings. A self-interested, secretive people, they adopt
human forms to influence events in their favor. A few use
their shapeshifting abilities to hunt humans in towns and
cities, while others orchestrate vast conspiracies to keep
themselves well fed and protected from discovery. They
enjoy manipulating mortals and construct elaborate ruses
to trick them, often with fatal consequences.
A broodling can pass for human, though close inspection
reveals the flaws in its disguise. Hairless and corpulent, with
waxy flesh, broodlings don’t quite fit into their clothes, and
they continually shed tiny worms and beetles. Many don dark
glasses to conceal their strange eyes, which never point in the
same direction. Should a broodling become injured, it sheds
its fleshy exterior and reveals its horrid true nature: a seething
cloud of gray flies rushes out from the deflating flesh.
Broodlings speak High Archaic and the Common Tongue.

Catoblepas
A catoblepas resembles a bison with thick armored plates
covering its back and a shaggy head equipped with two
small, curling horns. Despite their appearance, herds of
catoblepases are uncommon; most roam the Desolation
singly, scouring the landscape for the rare green growth
clumped around the few oases in the blasted lands.
Though normally docile, if threatened or surprised, a
catoblepas reacts with a blast of poisonous green vapor
from its nostrils that petrifies anything it kills.

Changeling
Called impostors, spies, and worse, changelings live in
fear of being discovered for what they truly are. They were
created by mischievous faerie to take the place of stolen
humans, and they live as those people until the magic that
made them begins to fail. In their true form, changelings
are often hideous, since their bodies are fashioned from
plants, dirt, bits of wood, and rock. For this reason, as well
as human distrust, changelings constantly wear disguises.
A changeling can become anyone it sees: a member of the
watch, a local priest, a bartender who knows the names
of all her patrons, a wizened elder, or a young child.
Changelings have trouble making meaningful connections
with others or developing interests independent of the
individuals whose forms they borrow. As a result, they
drift from one goal to the next, caring little whether they
accomplish it or not.
Humans know about changelings and ascribe all manner
of sinister qualities to them. In some lands, especially those
near the realms of faerie, people must submit to the test
of iron to prove they are what they appear to be. The test
is simple: merely take and hold a piece of iron. Faerie and
their kin cannot abide its touch and are impaired while
they remain in contact with it.
Most changelings speak the Common Tongue.

Clockworks typically speak the Common tongue. The

Construct
Constructs include a variety of creatures fashioned
from nonliving materials. A construct can have whatever
appearance its maker desires: it might be an ordinary
object animated by magic, a simulacrum of another
creature woven from threads of magic, or a machine
built in an engineer’s workshop to fulfill a specific
purpose.

A construct attacks with any part of its body that can
function as a weapon, or simply slams its body into
enemies. Those constructed to look like creatures might
use fists, horns, or feet. A wardrobe rams opponents or
batters them with its doors. An animated rug moves like
a serpent, rearing back and darting forward to pummel
enemies.

Demon
The Void belongs to the demons. These malevolent
shadows flit through the endless darkness and infest the
wreckage of the untold worlds destroyed by the Demon
Lord. As slaves to the Ender of All Things, evil and madness
consume these entities. Demons’ obsession with killing
and destroying makes them utterly unreasonable and
unpredictable.
Demons lack physical forms. Only when they enter
the universe do they gain bodies, almost always of a
horrid and monstrous aspect, as if assembled from
discarded parts by an idiotic and insane god.
Under their own power, demons cannot pierce the
boundary that separates the Eternal Darkness from the
universe beyond. They scour the edges for the rare gaps
where their master’s influence bleeds through or rely on
foolish mortals to summon them and let them loose to
visit ruin on the world. Once they have escaped the
Void, demons do not willingly return. Only the utter
annihilation of their physical forms or powerful
magic can cast them back whence they came.
Demons’ malevolent essence interacts with
the magic pervading the universe to create their
physical forms, so they are naturally resistant
to magical effects. They bring some of the Void’s
darkness with them when they materialize, plunging
their environs into shadow. Even so, their forms are
eerily visible; even creatures that cannot clearly see
them are subject to the demons’ horrifying trait.
Demonic Talent
Every demon takes on a unique appearance when
it materializes. The more powerful demons gain
unique abilities, represented by random rolls on
the Demonic Talents table. Instead of a demonic
talent, you can instead increase the demon’s
Health as directed in its statistics box.

Frenzied Attack The demon attacks two different targets
with its natural weapon, making each attack roll with
1 bane.
SPECIAL ACTIONS
Void Step The demon uses an action or a triggered action
on its turn to teleport to a space it can see within
medium range. Roll a d6. On a roll of 1, the demon cannot
use Void Step again for 1 minute.
Demonic Possession
If a creature goes mad as a result of gaining Insanity from
a demon’s horrifying trait, the demon can use a triggered
action to possess that creature. The demon makes a Will
attack roll against the triggering creature’s Will. On a success,
it disappears and enters the creature’s body, replacing the
creature’s Intellect and Will with its own and supplanting the
creature’s personality. The demon makes a prisoner of the
possessed creature’s soul and learns everything the creature
knows and remembers.
The demon can choose to hide within the possessed
creature, allowing the creature’s soul to take charge of the
body once again. The possessed creature has no recollection
of what happened while the demon was in control and does
not know of the possession. The demon can reassert control
at any time it chooses.
A creature possessed by a demon typically displays some
physical manifestation of the evil presence. It might reek
of rotting meat, expel foul substances, become sexually
aggressive, display weird markings on its flesh or assume an
unusual color, become afflicted with boils, sores, and bruises,
or have some other disturbing characteristic.
A possessing demon can be forced out of the creature’s
body, usually by magic. Once forced out, the demon must
make a Will challenge roll. On a success, it appears in an
open space of its choice within 10 yards of that creature. On a
failure, the demon disappears into the Void.

Bestiary
Demonic Talents
d20 Talent

Incarnation of Death The radius of the demon’s Demonic Shadows increases by 1 yard. At the end of each round, each
living creature in the area that is not a demon must make a Strength challenge roll. On a failure, the creature takes 2d6
damage.

Foment Discord Once per round, the demon can use a triggered action on its turn to make a Will attack roll against the
Will of one target creature within medium range of it. On a success, the target becomes consumed by hate for 1 round.
While consumed by hate, it must take the first turn it can and use an action to charge or make an attack with a weapon
against a target chosen by the demon.

Demon Seed When the demon gets an attack roll total of 20 or higher with its natural weapon and exceeds the target’s
Defense by 5 or more, it attempts to implant its seed in the target’s body. The target must make an Agility challenge roll
with 1 bane. On a failure, the target becomes implanted with a demon seed. The seed takes 1d6 rounds to mature. At the
end of each round until then, the target takes 1d6 damage and must make a Will challenge roll. On a failure, the target is
dazed from pain for 1 round. At the end of the round in which the seed matures, the target takes 3d6 damage and a tiny
demon tears free from its body, entering an open space within 1 yard of it.

Poisonous The demon’s claws, fangs, or other natural weapons drip with venom. It gains the poisonous trait (see
Customizing Creatures).

Dread The demon uses an action or a triggered action on its turn to send a wave of terror into an 8-yard-long cone
originating from a point it can reach. Each creature in the area must make a Will challenge roll. On a failure, the creature
gains 1 Insanity. If the creature is already frightened, it also becomes stunned for 1 minute. Once the demon uses Dread, it
cannot do so again for 1 hour.

Weapon of Chaos The demon wields a weapon of chaos, a manifestation of its dark will, in place of its natural weapon.
Attack rolls with this weapon are made with 1 boon, dealing 1d6 + its natural weapon damage. In addition, a creature
that takes damage from the weapon of chaos gains 1 Corruption.

Erratic At the end of each round, roll a d6. On an odd number, the demon is dazed for 1 round. On an even number, the
demon can take both a fast turn and a slow turn during the next round, making attack rolls and challenge rolls with 1 boon.

Legion The demon’s form is a fusion of several smaller demons. The first time it takes any damage, it collapses into a pile
of small demons. Divide the original demon’s Difficulty by 50 to determine how many appear; each enters an open space
within 1 yard of the original demon’s space and can take the next available turn. The new demons do not have this talent.

Stench At the end of each round, each living creature within short range of the demon must make a Strength challenge
roll. On a failure, the creature becomes impaired for 1 round.
10 Plague-Bearer The demon carries a loathsome disease. It gains the infectious trait (see Customizing Creatures).

Barbed Tendrils The demon uses an action to launch 1d6 barbed tendrils from its body, dividing them as it chooses
between any number of target creatures within short range of it. For each tendril, the demon makes a Strength attack
against the target’s Agility. On a success, the tendril punches into the target’s body, dealing 1d6 damage. Until it frees
itself, the target cannot move away from the demon and is pulled along (remaining at the same distance) if the demon
moves away from it. The target can free itself by destroying all the tendrils attached to it. Each tendril has Defense 5
and Health 5. Once the demon uses Barbed Tendrils, it cannot do so again for 1 hour.

Pincers When the demon gets a success on an attack roll using its natural weapon, it can use a triggered action to grab
the target.

Infested Tiny animals, such as rats or frogs, infest the demon’s body. When the demon takes damage from a weapon, 1d6
tiny animals spill out of it and attack the creature that damaged their host. Each enters an open space within 1 yard of the
demon’s space and can take the next available turn. Once the demon uses Infested, it cannot do so again for 1d6 rounds.

Spiked Tail The demon uses an action or a triggered action on its turn to make a Strength attack roll with 1 boon against
the Defense of one target creature within the demon’s reach + 1. On a success, the target takes 2d6 damage.

Flatulence The demon uses an action or a triggered action on its turn to expel a foul cloud of gas from its orifices.
The cloud spreads out in an 8-yard-long cone from a point the demon can reach. Each creature in the area must make
a Strength challenge roll. On a failure, the creature becomes poisoned while it remains in the cloud and for 1 round
after it leaves. While poisoned in this way, the creature is also dazed. Once the demon uses Flatulence, it cannot do
so again for 1 hour.
16 Wings The demon can fly at its listed speed.

Spellcaster (Minor) The demon has Power 1. Choose one tradition. The demon knows one rank 0 spell and two rank 1
spells from that tradition. If the demon already has a Spellcaster talent, instead increase the demon’s Health by 20.

Spellcaster (Major) The demon has Power 2. Choose one tradition. The demon knows one rank 0 spell, two rank 1 spells,
and one rank 2 spell from that tradition. If the demon already has this talent or a Spellcaster talent from a higher roll,
instead increase the demon’s Health by 20.

Spellcaster (Superior) The demon has Power 3. Choose one tradition. The demon knows one rank 0 spell, two rank 1
spells, two rank 2 spells, and one rank 3 spell from that tradition. If the demon already has this talent or a Spellcaster
talent from a higher roll, instead increase the demon’s Health by 20.

Spellcaster (Diverse) The demon has Power 3. Choose two traditions. The demon knows one rank 0 spell, one rank 1
spell, one rank 2 spell, and one rank 3 spell from each tradition. If the demon already has this talent, instead increase its
Health by 20.

Dire Wolf
Dreaded predators of the faerie realms, dire wolves
slip across the borders between the worlds to hunt, kill,
and feed. A dire wolf resembles an ordinary wolf but is
much larger, standing up to 5 feet at the shoulder. It has
humanoid features, thick with fur, and its forelegs end in
clawed hands.
Dire wolves cannot speak, but they understand Elvish.

Dragon
Dragons come in many different shapes and sizes. Some
have colorful or drab scales, while others feature hair,
spines, and other characteristics. All dragons have the same
general shape: a sinuous body with a long tail that extends
to about twice the body’s length. Two leathery wings extend
out from the shoulder blades, large enough to carry the
heavy creature into the air. A dragon’s large head tips a long,
flexible neck and boasts a crown of horns and an enormous
maw filled with sharp teeth. All dragons can belch up a
noxious fluid similar to naphtha that ignites when ejected
from their mouths.
Dragons can be found in all climates and terrains, from
coastal caves to the depths of forests to caverns deep under
the mountains. They are solitary creatures and emerge
from their lairs only to feed; they eat anything they catch.
Dragons prize shiny, glittering things, and many decorate
their lairs with fantastical treasures.

Drakes haunt the deep forests, hunting other predators.

Dread Mother
Dread mothers inhabit the most far-flung hinterlands
of the civilized world. They inspire terror as they wing
through the night skies, descending to feed and to deposit
their young in the living flesh of their victims. A dread
mother has a human-shaped form with great feathery
wings, similar to those of moths, spreading from its back.
It has shriveled arms and legs and a heavy abdomen
distended by the eggs it carries.
When a dread mother attacks, it flies toward a living
creature and unhinges its jaw to let loose a long, prehensile
tongue that ends in a sharp spike. The tongue injects a
toxin that renders its victim defenseless. The dread mother
squats over the fallen creature and uses a special organ to
implant the eggs inside the wound. Its belly now empty, the
monster flutters off to feed elsewhere, leaving its young to
eat their way free from the host.

DrYad
Dryads live in the depths of untamed woods. These willful,
capricious sprites dance through the trees, silvery laughter
echoing weirdly as they pass. They lure humans who catch
their fancy into their homes, imprisoning them for months
or years before releasing the captives from their charms.
Dryads hide within their chosen trees unless they choose
to reveal themselves; finding one that doesn’t want to be
discovered is almost impossible. When a dryad steps forth,
it resembles a young and beautiful woman, with pointed
ears, glittering eyes, and hair that matches the colors of the
leaves on its tree.
Dryads speak Elvish.

Dwarf
Dwarfs delve deep into the earth, digging for gold, silver,
gemstones, and other treasures from the unyielding stone.
A people of short stature and broad build, they are strong
and hardy, able to withstand the hardships of their work
and the depths into which they descend. Most dwarfs,
both male and female, have extensive facial hair, which
they wear in beards and mustaches braided or greased into
fanciful shapes. Dwarfs have long memories and never
forget a slight. They despise goblins and trolls, and their
grudges sometimes impel them to attack on sight.
Legend holds the dwarfs were not always as they are
today. Grimnir, their maker, fashioned them to be tall,
beautiful, and powerful. But their vanity was the dwarfs’
undoing. They saw the gods not as their masters, but as
their rivals. They built a great tower to climb through
the skies so they could lay siege to heaven and take the
gods’ thrones for themselves. For their hubris, Grimnir
cursed them. He stripped from them their beauty and
stature, leaving them and all their descendants a stunted,
embittered people. The god doomed them to grub for the
treasures of earth instead of seeking the glories of heaven,
and so all dwarfs are born with a lust for gold and gems.
Dwarfs speak Dwarfish and the Common Tongue.

Elf
The lords and ladies of the hidden kingdoms, elves
abandoned the mortal world long ago for the wondrous
realms spun into being with their great magical power, such as
Alfheim or the Lands of the Ever Young. A few retreated into
the deep wilderness, unwilling to surrender their homelands
to the talking beasts that stink of iron. Most elves prefer their
isolation, but some leave the bright lands to walk in the world
and gaze with wonder or horror on mortal works.
Elves are slender and comely people, with heart-shaped
faces, canted eyes, pointed ears, and androgynous features.
They dress in clothing made from strange and impossible
materials such as shadows, moonbeams, or a lover’s breath.

Fury
Furies fly out from the depths of Hell to visit doom on
oathbreakers and traitors, on their own or at the behest
of their infernal masters. Once a fury sets its sights on a
victim, it pursues the offending mortal to the ends of the
earth, determined to drag the soul to Hell.

braids. They would be beautiful were it not for the hatred
contorting their features. All furies wield fiery swords.

Genie
When the universe sprang into
existence eons ago, it brought with it
bodiless entities, awakened
by creation’s magic. Such
spirits usually drift through
the worlds, unseen, unfelt,
unnoticed but for a tingling of
the skin, a sensation of someone
or something nearby, or a faint
noise that has no obvious source.
Genies live in dancing flames,
stirring breezes, hulking mountains,
and crashing waves, heedless of the
oblivious mortals.
Rarely do genies trouble other
creatures, unless compelled by magic.
Practitioners of elemental magic summon
them to learn the spells that manipulate these primal
forces. When summoned, a genie assumes a physical
form infused with elemental power to become a wild,
dangerous entity.

What at first looks like a stack of rocks and dirt reveals its
true nature when it moves. The rocks making up the genie’s

spilling from its earthen form. Black chips of glittering

Bestiary
Ghastly Chorus
A ghastly chorus is made from stripping the faces of a dozen
or more victims from their skulls and fusing them into a
sheet of stretched skin. It moves by fluttering and lurching
over the ground, eyes flicking back and forth, its many
mouths yawning wide as they whisper dire secrets of the
afterlife.
Ghastly choruses lurk in old ruins and cemeteries,
where dabblers in the dark arts ruminate over the
forbidden knowledge they have accumulated.
The chorus serves its maker as a herald,
announcing the sovereignty of its master to
any who stumble into the lair.
The deboned heads used to create a ghastly
chorus retain scraps of memory from their lives.
Their mouths whisper or shriek in the Common
Tongue or, rarely, High Archaic. The abomination
craves conversation and gibbers madly at anyone who
will listen, lashing out violently at those who won’t. Its mad
pronouncements and horrific appearance assault mortal
minds, leaving their owners gasping in terror.

Ghoul
Most societies forbid humans to knowingly feed on other
humans. To do so invites a horrid curse: transformation
into a ghoul.
Ghouls are corpse-eaters, shunned for their unspeakable
appetites. They prowl graveyards, breaking into tombs
and digging up coffins to get at the choice morsels within.
Eternally hungry, ghouls eat any flesh, no matter how
rancid or putrid. However, when given the choice, they
favor fresh meat pulled from the bones of children.
A ghoul adopts the likeness of the last creature it ate. As
its unholy appetite grows, it reverts to its usual gaunt and
sickly form, its crusted maw filled with pointed black teeth
and a forked, sore-ridden tongue.
Ghouls speak the Common Tongue.

Speed 8

against a creature wearing or wielding a holy symbol.

Drink Blood on attack roll 20+)

blood, it takes 1d6 extra damage and becomes fatigued
for 1 minute. While fatigued in this way, the target is
also slowed. If it was already fatigued, it instead takes
another 1d6 extra damage.
SPECIAL ACTIONS

reach, which requires concentrating for 1 minute. At
the end of this time, the ghoul utterly consumes the
corpse and assumes the creature’s appearance for 24
hours. While wearing this new form, the ghoul loses its
frightening trait.

Bestiary
Giant
Giants are primitive, backward, and incredibly stupid.
They pay little attention to where they go and leave a trail
of smashed houses, flattened wagons, and partly eaten
livestock when wandering through settled lands.
A typical giant stands about 15 feet tall and weighs about
2,000 pounds. It looks like an enormous human with a
slouched posture and exaggerated features: a broad nose,
drooping eyebrows, and a slack mouth filled with stained
teeth the size of shields. Most giants eschew clothing,
though the more modest might strap livestock, living or
dead, over their nether regions, or don carnival tents.
Giants speak the Trollish language. More intelligent
giants might also know the Common Tongue.

Goblin
Cast out from the realms of faerie long ago, goblins now
make their way in the mortal world. They occupy the
bottom rung of the social ladder, performing the work no
one else is willing to do. Many goblins delight in making
mischief, and the worst of their kind live as thieves,
scoundrels, and troublemakers.
Goblins reproduce like rats. They live in crowded
conditions in underground warrens, often in human cities,
using scraps and stolen materials. No two goblins are exactly
alike. Most stand around 3 feet tall and weigh about 40 or 50
pounds, but all have a unique characteristic that sets them
apart. Horns, fangs, snouts, tails, blotchy skin, extra digits or
eyes, and worse mar their forms.
Goblins speak the Common Tongue and Elvish.

Golem
Golems are massive, lumbering beings formed from clay
and animated by magic to serve their creators. Prized for
their great strength and their obedience, golems carry
out whatever instructions they receive to the letter. A
golem might spend a century digging a tunnel through a
mountain or stand guard for a thousand lifetimes without
growing tired or feeling the need to do anything else. Each
golem abides by a list of three rules, unique to itself, that its
maker has inscribed inside its head.

Bestiary
Gorgon
The Witch-King created the gorgons from his brides, whose
beauty was unmatched by any in the world. He gifted
them with eternal life, but to keep their vanity in check, he
also cursed them, transforming them into monstrosities
whose gaze turned the living to stone statues. Somehow,
the gorgons survived the Witch-King’s defeat and scattered
across the Empire’s lands.
An echo of the beauty that earned their place as the
Witch-King’s brides still lingers in gorgons’ shapely upper
bodies and striking features. But the rest of their forms are
monstrous: crowns of eyeless serpents emerge from their
heads and long serpent tails replace their legs.
Gorgons dwell in old ruins, under cities, or in remote
wilderness areas where they pass the endless years in
isolation. Some offer guidance to mortals who dare
approach, conferring on them the wisdom accumulated
over their long lives.
A gorgon’s gaze retains power for 1d6 days after the
gorgon dies, provided its eyes remain intact. A creature
wielding the gorgon’s head can subject others to the
gorgon’s Petrifying Appearance and Petrifying Gaze.
Gorgons communicate in High Archaic.

the creature gains 1 Insanity, cannot avert its eyes from the
gorgon, and becomes slowed for a number of rounds equal
to the creature’s Insanity total. Whether it gets a success or a
failure, it cannot again be affected by that gorgon’s Petrifying
Appearance until after that creature completes a rest.

with 3 banes if it averted its eyes. On a failure, the
target takes 2d6 damage, becomes poisoned for
1 minute, and cannot avert its eyes for 1 round.
If the target is already poisoned in this way, it

END OF THE ROUND

move up to its Speed before or after the action.
Grave Thrall
Grave thralls haunt old battlefields, clinging to the mortal
world to complete some unfinished task. Their bodies are
worm-eaten, with tattered bits of skin hanging from their bones
and blue pinpricks of light glowing in their empty eye sockets.
Grave thralls do not speak, though they understand those
who have the power to command them.

Gremlin
Cunning mischief-makers, gremlins delight in creating
chaos. Their mere presence causes even the best-laid
plans to go awry. Gremlins followed the goblins out of the
Hidden Kingdoms and now wreak havoc on human cities.
Explosions, misfires, and constructs that behave erratically
are all signs of a gremlin infestation.
Technology attracts gremlins. A gremlin wants nothing
more than to take a device apart to see how it works. When
it puts it back together again, though, the item never seems
to work quite right and has a tendency to break at the most
inopportune times.

Hag
Nymphs are wilderness faerie of surpassing beauty.
But when a nymph’s joy becomes sorrow and bitterness
replaces happiness, hate causes the nymph’s beauty to
wither and die. What’s left is a horror called a hag. Green-
skinned and warty, it is a monstrous reflection of the
nymph’s former self, intent on making everyone else as
miserable as itself.

Halfling
Halflings are diminutive farmers living on the outskirts of
human cities. Their idyllic communities, neat and orderly,
produce much of the foodstuffs on which human nations
depend. Halflings pride themselves in their work, live simply,
and have few ambitions beyond enjoying the time afforded
to them. They are fiercely independent and self-sufficient.
Halflings are cousins to humans, similar in all ways except
height. They stand about 3 feet tall and weigh about 50 pounds.
Halflings have the same range of coloration that humans have.
Halflings speak the Common Tongue.

Harpy
Sweet, alluring voices call travelers to their destruction.
They belong to the harpies, a hideous race of accursed
faerie that despise mortals and feed on any they get in
their grasp. Harpies have the wings, tails, and talons of
ravens merged with the torso of nymphs. Beneath the
feces, blood, and hateful behavior, harpies are quite
beautiful.
The harpies were once the loveliest of the nymphs, but
with great beauty came great vanity. They believed they
were greater and more alluring than the Faerie Queen
herself. The Faerie Queen, upon hearing of their boasting,
dismissed them from her court and sent them flying away
as ravens, whose shape still disfigures their forms.
Harpies speak Elvish.

Harvester
Harvesters haunt the Empire’s oldest cities. Direct
descendants of some ancient society, most likely struck
down by offended gods, they perpetuate their existence by
stealing what they need from humans. When something
breaks in a harvester’s body, it replaces the defective
part with whatever it can take until it looks like it has
been cobbled together from a dozen or more creatures.
Harvesters hide their grotesqueness behind heavy clothing
to help them move among their victims without attracting
attention to themselves.

reach, killing the creature instantly. The filch gains a 2d6
bonus to Health until it completes a rest.
SPECIAL ACTIONS
Skittering Dance The filch uses an action or a triggered
action on its turn to move up to its Speed. This
movement does not trigger free attacks.
Organ filches scour the shadowed streets of densely
populated cities for vagrants from which they harvest
fresh parts to replace their failing organs. They open up
their victims with long scalpels and carry bottles filled
with preservative fluid to hold their harvests until they
can return to their lairs and install the stolen flesh in their
bodies.
An organ filch goes about covered by a hooded canvas
cloak that is stained with blood from previous hunts.
Beneath is a ghastly figure wrapped in snug linens and
wearing elaborate headgear fitted with lenses to help it
perform surgery.
Organ filches speak High Archaic.

Harvesters discovered that replacing every part
of their bodies numbed their ability to feel and to
experience emotion. After extensive study, they learned to
concoct an elixir made from human tears that lets them
feel again, if only for a short while. Tear thieves extract
tears by causing their victims to experience horrific pain.
A tear thief wears black leather clothing along with a
heavy coat, white gloves, a top hat, and black lenses over its
eyes. It carries a thin knife with a serrated edge designed to
maximize the victim’s suffering.
Tear thieves speak High Archaic.
Hell Swine
Hell swine are a breed of ill-tempered hogs that grow to
obscene size. Vicious and temperamental, they destroy
their habitats and kill just about anything they can catch.
Hell swine have thick, leathery hides, gleaming red eyes,
and tufts of black hair rising from their backs. They gore
their foes with their sharp tusks.
Beastmen have had some success in training hell swine
to serve as steeds, though the beasts are unreliable and can
turn on riders with no warning.

Hobgoblin
Cousins to the exiled goblins, hobgoblins remain in the
hidden kingdoms of the faerie, where they live as slaves to
the elf lords and ladies. They are given to frequent bouts
of madness that manifest as random acts of senseless
violence, and often fight on the front lines in defense of the
faerie realms.
Unlike goblins, who have wildly varied appearances,
hobgoblins are identical, regardless of gender. Each one
stands exactly 5 feet, 4½ inches tall and weighs 166 pounds.
All have thick bellies, spindly limbs, and heavy jowls that
hang to their shoulders.
Hobgoblins speak Elvish.

Hood
Hoods were created by a secret society known as the Cabal
of the Black Sun, a largely forgotten group of dark wizards
set on finding immortality. They employ hoods as spies,
thieves, and assassins.
Hoods haunt city streets on fell errands for their
inscrutable masters. They don heavy black cloaks that
seem to drink the light and render them nearly invisible
when in shadows or darkness. They say little and seem
skilled in magic.
The few who have managed to see a hood clearly report it
has craggy features covered by a thick mustache and beard,
much like a dwarf. Only removing their cloaks reveals the
awful truth about hoods’ nature. Rather than skulls, they
have great glass orbs filled with murky liquid. Lamprey-
like creatures swim inside the glass vessels, presumably
controlling the hoods’ actions.
Hoods speak High Archaic.

Killing mist appears as a great bank of red-tinged fog that
spills over the ground, plunging the world into pale gloom
as it creeps along. In its depths one can make out weird,
distorted images of impossible shapes accompanied by mad
laughter and strings of words in a deep, muttering voice.
The killing mist never lingers long, dissipating almost as
quickly as it appeared. In the clearing air, one might spot a
few pale, dry bones, all that remains of the unlucky victims
of the entity’s repast.
Killing mist typically conceals itself inside a larger bank
of mundane fog, looking like a particularly dense region of
mist. It haunts shorelines and the surface of waters where
doldrums are common.

Clinging to walls and ceilings, lash crawlers might pass
for spiders. Close observation, though, reveals that their
bodies are bloated, pulsing eyeballs, each suspended on
seven long, hair-like legs. Lash crawlers spontaneously
appear in places scarred by reckless magic and feed on
the energy of living creatures to sustain their unnatural
existence.
Lash crawlers gather in small groups of five to ten in
caves and ruins, usually in places that have endured
bombardment from wild and chaotic magic.

Leshy
The leshy walk the primeval forests, tending to the trees
and encouraging saplings to grow tall and strong. Leshy
dislike humans for their carelessness but despise orcs and
other filthy creatures that wantonly burn and destroy. Leshy
sometimes join forces with druids against a common enemy.
A leshy looks like a tree of any species, though oak is
most common. A leshy that stands still is indistinguishable
from a normal tree and might hold this position for
decades. When it does move, the lower trunk splits into
long legs. The leshy’s face peers out from the center of its
trunk, and it can bend its branches to use as arms.
A leshy typically speaks the Common Tongue and Elvish,
and it can communicate with any plant within 100 yards of it.

Living Tar
Living tar is a mobile slick of black slime that creeps
toward anything it detects with its weird senses. It
gathers up its body into pseudopods with which it
smashes prey, then absorbs their vital fluids.
Some believe that living tar is the essence of slain demons
trapped in the mortal world.

Lizardman
Before humanity’s rise, visitors from another dimension
traveled through the Void to establish colonies in this
world. A reptilian race, with vast knowledge of magic,
science, and technology, they built cities whose ruins can
still be found in remote corners of the world or buried deep
underground. Not much is known of them or their society,
but sages speculate some calamity caused their collapse
and sent the survivors sliding into savagery. Their brutish
descendants can still be found in the bogs and swamps
of the old Empire and north, in the steaming jungles that
spread across much of that region.
Lizardmen stand about 7 feet tall and weigh around 250
pounds. Olive, brown, or black scales cover their bodies,
fading to tan on their chests. Most forgo clothing, though
warlocks in their communities sometimes wear ceremonial
robes decorated with weird glyphs and sigils.
Lizardmen speak their own language, a sibilant, hissing
tongue.

A lurk looks like a bipedal lizard with a mottled gray-

rows of six eyes march up either side of its head, each eye
moving independently. A lurk’s forelimbs end in long,

Manes
Death frees the mortal soul from the physical body. Souls that
sink into the Underworld become manes and pass the years in
the dark and somber place, their memories gradually fading
until nothing of their identities remains, at which point the
souls travel back to the mortal world to live again.
When a manes first appears in the Underworld, it has the
form it wore in life, albeit ashy, with dark circles around its
eyes. As the years pass, its distinctive appearance begins to
fade, leaving behind a pale, almost featureless humanoid
shape. If attacked, the manes’s fingers lengthen into claws
and its mouth yawns wide to issue an awful keening.
Manes speak the Common Tongue or High Archaic.

black wings and a scorpion’s tail that drips venom. Instead of
a lion’s head it has a monstrous human visage, twisted into a
bestial grimace. Manticores hunt and eat humans. They must
feed several times each night to appease their terrible hunger.
Many manticores learn a few words of the Common
Tongue, often those cried out by their victims in their last
moments. They mockingly parrot those words in guttural
voices as they terrorize new prey.

teeth, the gaps clotted with bits of rotting
flesh and caked with yellow-white plaque.
A muttering maw lumbers about on
elephantine legs and swings club-like
appendages ending in three-fingered
hands that grab creatures and stuff
them into its maw.

Bestiary
Nisse
The elves withdrew from the mortal world far ahead of
humanity’s tide, but not all faerie went with them. A few
remained, unwilling to retreat to realms of dream and illusion.
Among them were the nisse, who haunt the wilderness still.
Nisse roam the frontiers of human lands, watching
mortals, weighing their actions, and judging them. In
winter, nisse might deliver gifts to human and halfling
families who have shown respect for the old ways and
ancient places, depositing tokens on their doorsteps.
A nisse looks like a tiny old man, 6 inches tall, bent with
the weight of years and hobbling with the support of a tiny
twig. It has a long white beard that drags along the ground.
Nisse wear scarlet clothing that consists of a heavy coat and a
tall, pointed cap. Some keep pigs as companions and steeds.
Nisse speak the Common Tongue and Elvish.

Oculus
A quivering red eye drifts across a slick of greenish-yellow
slime, reeking of sickness and disease. Visible in its
membranous body are floating scraps of skin and pieces of
bone. Oculi bubble into the world through mirrors warped
by the Demon Lord’s influence.
Dimly sentient, oculi relentlessly search for flesh to
eat. When one discovers something edible, it flows over
the prey to dissolve the meat and bones with its corrosive
secretions. Its horrific appearance can pin potential prey in
place, greatly easing the process.

Bestiary
Ogre
Ogres think about little else other than the rumbling in
their prodigious bellies. They stuff their maws with what
they catch, gobbling flesh, bone, armor, dirt, and offal,
ending the meal with a thundering belch. Within moments
of eating, an ogre heads off in search of something else to
devour. Having no lands of their own, ogres wander, feed,
and then move on, leaving behind great steaming piles of
excrement.
Ogres stand about 9 feet tall. Filth crusts their mottled
and sore-dimpled hides. They drape their bodies with
rubbish they find, such as furs, tents, banners, and tarps.
They are prone to mutation and often sport all manner of
unusual physical features.
Ogres speak Trollish.

Vomit When the ogre takes damage, it can use a

a 3-yard-long cone originating from a point it can
reach. Each creature in the area must make an Agility
challenge roll. A creature takes 2d6 damage and
becomes impaired for 1 round on a failure, or just takes
half the damage on a success.
		 Once the ogre uses Vomit, it cannot do so again until
after it eats.

Ooze
Oozes are predatory slicks of transparent or translucent
slime that creep and slide across surfaces in pursuit of
prey. They feed by dissolving their prey and
absorbing nutrients from the liquefied
remains.
Oozes come in a wide variety of
colors, from gray or black to brown
to bright green, and can range in
size from harmless droplets to
pools 4 or 5 yards in diameter.

Orc
Centuries ago, the Empire’s dark wizards used magic to
transform slaves into orcs, an obedient race of warriors.
The Empire relied on orcs to enforce laws and keep order
for centuries. They proved a fecund race, though, and their
numbers quickly outgrew the Empire’s ability to house
and feed them. To keep their numbers in control, orcs were
“retired” on their thirtieth birthday, shipped off to secret
camps deep underground where they were slaughtered.
Their remains, ground up into meal, fed the other orc
soldiers. Eventually they rose against their masters, and
orcs now seek their own destiny.
An orc stands about 6 feet tall and can weigh up to 300
pounds. It has pronounced bone ridges above the eyes, a
short nose, and a wide mouth filled with sharp teeth. Orcs
have blotchy skin marred with open, weeping sores, and
thick hair on their heads and faces and
across much of their bodies.
Orcs adorn themselves
with grotesque spoils of
war, such as a bundle of
severed heads hanging from
a belt, a necklace of fingers
tied around the neck, or
the faces of dead enemies
nailed to armor.

Phantom
Sudden, unexpected death can leave souls anchored in
the mortal world, moored by some task left unfinished, a
loved one unguarded, or some magic whose hold cannot be
broken. Those with strong personalities become phantoms,
ghostly versions of their former selves trapped between the
realms of the living and the dead.
A phantom looks somewhat like it did in life, but its
transparent form glows faintly with eerie green light. The
true shape of its body is indistinct, with blurred edges.
Phantoms speak the Common Tongue or High Archaic.

Poltergeist
The trauma of death is only made worse when the soul
refuses to move on to the Underworld. It clings to the
mortal realm for fear of losing what it was, forgetting what
it had known, and fading from the world. Such refusal
turns to resentment for the living; when the resentment
blossoms into hate, a poltergeist results.

---

Bestiary
These “noisy ghosts” haunt places inhabited by the
living. They watch from the shadows and peer through
windows, sometimes appearing in a mirror’s reflection
or leaving a handprint on a frosty window. The longer
a poltergeist spends around the living, the angrier it
becomes until it begins trying to drive away what it sees
as intruders. A haunting begins with soft knocks, opening
and closing doors, or vile messages scrawled in dust or
chalked on the walls. If the inhabitants refuse to leave, the
poltergeist escalates the effort by hurling dishes, stacking
chairs, rearranging rooms, and more. Usually, such
displays are enough to panic the living.
It takes great effort for a poltergeist to show itself, so
it rarely does so. When it manifests, it takes the form it
had as a living person, usually sporting grievous injuries.
Poltergeists speak in whispers or communicate with
disturbing messages left in the places they haunt.

Promethean
Fashioned out of body parts harvested from dead creatures
and restored to life by strange magic or weird science,
a promethean exists in a state of perpetual torment. Its
mind is assailed by memories from a life it can only dimly
remember, its sanity pushed to the breaking point by the
horror of its existence. Prometheans grudgingly serve their
makers, but if pushed too far, they might rebel, lashing out
to destroy everything around them.
Prometheans understand the Common Tongue but do
not speak.

Bestiary
Redcap
The most malicious and cruel of the faerie, redcaps take
their name for the sodden hats they wear on their heads.
They drench these caps in human blood that drips and
spatters on their clothing. They must perform this ritual
and keep their caps wet or they die.
Redcaps look like little old men, gnarled and twisted,
with glittering eyes beneath beetling brows. Large yellow
teeth crowd their mouths, and streaks of blood run down
their faces and clot in their white beards. Redcaps wear
heavy boots and carry razors to slit their victims’ throats.
Redcaps speak Elvish and know a few words of the
Common Tongue.

Reen
The reen do not belong in the world. They are invaders
from another universe, one imperiled by the Demon Lord.
The people from that world dispatch reen into the Void to
locate a suitable world on which they might start again and
to prepare the way.
A reen looks like a tangle of metallic, segmented
tentacles that meet at a central ball with a single, glowing
red eye. It flies through the air or pulls itself along with its
tentacles.
Whether or not reen understand spoken languages is
unclear, since they ignore efforts to communicate with
them. They use lethal force without provocation, though
they sometimes take a moment to study their kills.

Bestiary
Rot Maiden
From a distance, a rot maiden looks like a seated young
woman, head down and hidden by what seems to be a
veil. Appearances are deceiving, though. A rot maiden is
actually a strange, immobile fungus that lures the unwary
to their deaths by the spores it emits. These spores have an
enticing aroma that few can resist. When a victim draws
near, the rot maiden raises its “head” and disorients its prey
with a psychic attack, then launches filaments to infect
victims with flesh-eating poison. The virulent poison turns
flesh and bone into a stinking slime that enriches the soil
around the maiden’s perch.

While impaired this way, the creature is also slowed.
		 Once the rot maiden uses Part the Veil, it cannot do so
again for 1 minute.

creature in the area that is not a fungus must make a
Strength challenge roll with 1 bane. On a failure, the creature
gains 1 Insanity and becomes compelled for 1 round.
Shadow
A shadow is a soul bearing the stain of the Demon Lord that
slips free from the realms of the dead, sustaining its unnatural
existence by feeding on the living. Shadows loathe all life and
delight in corrupting new souls to add to their numbers.
Shadows take many forms. Some look like blots of
darkness or undulating masses of gloom. Others display
hints of who they once were in their shape and physical
characteristics, while yet others assume more monstrous
shapes that display the range of horrific traits found in
demons of the Void.

Perception 13 (+3); darksight
Defense 14; Health 20; Insanity 1; Corruption 7

Speed 10

asleep, blinded, deafened, diseased, fatigued,
immobilized, poisoned, slowed

makes while the target has this penalty, the creature
dies. At the end of the next round, a new shadow
wriggles free from the body and stands up in the nearest
open space. The shadow can take the next available turn.
END OF THE ROUND
Burned by Sunlight The shadow takes 2d6 damage if it is
in an area lit by sunlight.

Bestiary
Shadow Weaver
Webs choke the remains of the lost city, pale strands
stretching between high towers and across the tangled
streets. Wisps of the sticky stuff hang in the air, blown
about by the fetid breeze. Such places are home to shadow
weavers, a race of intelligent spiders wholly in the thrall
of the Demon Lord. Shadow weavers hunt humans and
other sentient creatures, paralyzing them with poison
and then encasing them in sticky cocoons for later
consumption.
A shadow weaver has a glossy black body with a bulbous
abdomen. Bright red numbers glow all over the carapace,
but if these have any significance, the monsters have never
revealed it.
Shadow weavers work in small groups that follow
prey moving into their territory, creeping through
the shadows and waiting for the right time to strike.
They sometimes taunt their prisoners in Dark Speech,
whispering of the terrifying things they will do before
devouring them.

damage, gains 1 Corruption, and becomes poisoned
for 1 minute. While poisoned this way, the target is
immobilized. If it is already poisoned, it instead takes
another 2d6 extra damage and becomes defenseless
for 1 minute.

at any time using a triggered action. The strand has

area obscured by shadows or darkness, it can use a
triggered action to automatically become hidden.
Shrieking Eel
Shrieking eels resemble ordinary eels but grow up to 12
feet long. They take their name for the alarming noise
they make when they detect prey, signaling other eels to
join the attack.

Skinchanger
Skinchangers hide in plain sight among ordinary people,
who do not suspect their neighbor, lover, friend, or family
member bears a terrible curse. But when the moon rises
full, a change comes over the accursed one, transforming it
into a horrible monster until moonset. It becomes a wild,
savage killer, driven by an insatiable need to eat the flesh of
the living.
Skinchangers can adopt one of two other forms in
addition to their human appearance. One is that of an
animal, usually a wolf, though bears, lions, boars, giant rats,
and others are possible. In this form, the skinchanger is
physically indistinguishable from other animals of its kind,
though it behaves strangely and is unusually aggressive.
The second form is a hybrid that combines features of the
animal and humanoid shapes.
Only mortal, human-shaped creatures are susceptible to
the skinchangers’ curse—humans, halflings, dwarfs, and
the like.
SKINCHANGER DIFFICULTY 25
Size 1/2 or 1 frightening monster
Perception 13 (+3); shadowsight
Defense 15; Health 30; Insanity 4; Corruption 2
Strength 14 (+4), Agility 12 (+2), Intellect 9 (–1), Will 11 (+1)
Speed 12
Silver Vulnerability When a skinchanger takes damage
from a silver weapon, it takes a penalty to Health equal
to the damage. The penalty lasts until the skinchanger
completes a rest.
ATTACK OPTIONS
Teeth (melee; hybrid form only) +4 with 2 boons (3d6 plus
Skinchanger Curse)
Skinchanger Curse If the target is human or a similar
mortal creature and becomes incapacitated by the
skinchanger’s attack but does not die, it must make a
Strength challenge roll with 1 bane the next time the
moon rises full. On a failure, the target transforms into
a skinchanger until moonset. While transformed, it uses
the skinchanger’s attributes, characteristics, attacks,
talents, and traits in place of its own but can take only
hybrid form. When the transformation ends, the target
has no memory of its time as a skinchanger.
		 The curse lasts until lifted or until the target kills the
skinchanger that cursed it.

traits. It retains its own Intellect and Will.

Spriggan
People who explore the borders between the mortal world
and the hidden kingdoms of the faerie sometimes report
encountering strange, violent folk of the wood that attack
without provocation and seem intent on driving interlopers
away. These beings are spriggans, magical creations of the
Fair Folk tasked with protecting their borders and places
important to their kind.
A spriggan stands about 5 feet tall and has a willowy,
humanoid shape made from twisting vines and thorny
branches. It has sparse facial features, little more than a
pair of glowing green eyes.
Spriggans understand Elvish but do not speak.

Stone Worm
Stone worms burrow through the earth, surfacing to snatch
livestock or people and drag them into the subterranean
darkness. A profusion of deep craters mark places infested
with these relentless hunters. From the depths rises the
stench of rotting meat mingled with an odd cinnamon smell.
A stone worm can grow up to 24 feet long and have a
diameter of up to 6 feet. Its segmented body has a thick,
rubbery hide, mottled brown and gray. Thin slime oozes
from the creases between the segments and a great,
yawning maw dominates its scarred head, filled with sharp,
inward-pointing teeth.

takes 2d6 damage from the worm’s digestive juices. If
the worm becomes incapacitated, it vomits forth any
creatures it has swallowed. Each lands prone in an open
space within 1 yard of the worm.

heaving swarms that can strip a living creature down to

stripe running down the center of its shell.

Troglodyte
Troglodytes abandoned their humanity when they fled into
the bowels of the earth to escape justice for their wicked
acts. They survived for generations in the noisome dark,
becoming more and more inbred until they were reduced to
a gibbering mob.
Troglodytes have hairless, chalk-white skin crusted with
filth and blood. Bruises ring their black eyes, and they
file their teeth to sharp points. They rarely bother to wear
clothing and instead paint their bodies with white mud.
Troglodytes speak a debased form of High Archaic
peppered with words and phrases from Dark Speech.

Bestiary
Troll
Trolls have lived in the world almost as long as the faerie.
A hateful, spiteful race, they despise the Fair Folk for their
beauty, mischief, and joy. In ancient times, they fought
bloody, disastrous wars against their foes until the Faerie
Queen, sickened by the carnage, stripped them of their
magic and left them vulnerable to the sun’s purifying light.
The accursed trolls retreated to deep valleys and dug into
caves under mountains and hills to escape the hateful light.
Thus began their rapid decline into madness and savagery,
until they became little more than lumbering brutes filled
with a dim hatred for all living things.
A typical troll stands 10 feet tall and weighs 750 pounds.
It has a stooped body, a bulbous nose, and a wide mouth
filled with chisel-like teeth. Most trolls have patches of
petrified flesh from brief encounters with the sun. They
wear animal hides as clothing.
All trolls speak Trollish, and most know a little Elvish
and the Common Tongue.
TROLL DIFFICULTY 250
Size 2 troll
Perception 15 (+5); darksight
Defense 16; Health 110 (Regeneration); Insanity 1; Corruption 3

the troll turns into a statue and dies.
Regeneration The troll heals 1d6 + 2 damage if it is not
incapacitated.
Vampire
Vampires rule the night. When the sun sinks beneath the
horizon, they emerge from their tombs to stalk the living,
drawing them close with magic and draining their blood.
Vampires possess great power but have several fatal flaws that
bold hunters can exploit. For this reason, vampires show great
restraint even though they constantly thirst for fresh blood.
A vampire can create a “child” by draining a victim to the
point that it starts dying. It feeds the creature some of the
vampire’s own blood, killing the victim almost immediately,
then inters the corpse in a tomb, vault, coffin, or somewhere
else the sun cannot reach. The corpse rises as a new
vampire at the next sunset and is compelled until released
or until its maker is destroyed.
The process of becoming undead leaves a vampire
somewhat unhinged, and many develop irrational
superstitions. They might recoil from mirrors, compulsively
count everything they see, be repulsed by the stench of
garlic, or retreat from a brandished holy symbol. None of
these things cause real harm to a vampire and, in time, it
might overcome its superstition.
Vampires speak High Archaic and the Common Tongue.

Perception 16 (+6); darksight
Defense 20; Health 90; Insanity —; Corruption 5

diseased, fatigued, immobilized, poisoned, slowed

damage or makes an attack roll, at which point its
features contort to assume a monstrous appearance. The
vampire retains this appearance until it uses an action to
resume its human appearance. While it appears human,
the vampire loses its horrifying trait.

Characters
In addition to the creatures described here, player
characters might encounter other people, many of whom
can be just as dangerous as monsters. All the characters
described in this section are assumed to be human, though
they can have any ancestry you want without significantly
altering their statistics.
Characters speak the languages of their homelands.
Educated characters might also read and write one or
more languages.

working to combat corruption’s spread and fight agents
sworn to the Demon Lord.

Cultist
In uncertain times, some people look for divine beings
to ease their fears and grant them hope that they will
somehow survive the catastrophes ravaging their lives. Most
turn to the established religions, finding comfort in the

succor.
Cultists include any groups of like-minded individuals
pledged to serve a mysterious power that might or might
