```text
Hujeta
After several uprisings against the Hegemony, the Witch-
King commanded his demonologists to create tireless
spies to search out disloyal subjects and destroy them.
Months later, the demonologists returned with the hujeta,
a breed of demon that could stay aloft indefinitely and
came equipped with keen eyesight capable of discerning
the smallest details. Although difficult to create, scores of
them constantly patrolled the skies over much of Ashrakal’s
kingdom, neutralizing many threats before they could
bring harm to the new order.
Hujeta resemble large ravens, but with a single giant,
swiveling eyeball in place of a head, and wingspans of
sixteen feet. The demons could shine a fell light from their
eyes and anything illuminated became rooted to the spot,
allowing allies on the ground to find and capture whoever
was being pursued.

Pyron
The Gog demonologists released pyrons ahead of the main
forces to crash into the lead ranks of enemy soldiers, setting
enemy combatants aflame and shrouding the battlefield
with thick, choking smoke. Pyrons appear as blackened
skeletons wreathed in flame. Smoke billows from their
burning bodies, blinding their opponents and making it
difficult to breathe. The intensely hot flames from their
bodies leap and dance, setting fire to anything nearby. For
those opponents not yet ignited, the pyrons have long,
curling claws extending from their bony hands, also aflame,
which they use to slice and sear through flesh and bone.

Scions of Gog
After their great defeat at the hands of the Kalasans, those
Men of Gog who survived scattered across the continent.
Some, horribly corrupted by the dark and forbidden
magic they wielded, had offspring who became degenerate
monsters, troglodytes, mogs, and worse. Back in the old
kingdom beyond the wastes of the Desolation, those who did
not answer Ashrakal’s call, or fled back there after his defeat,
now find themselves, ironically, slaves to the tyranny of the
Death Lords who rule over them from their Obsidian Vaults.
Quite a few, however, remained within the new Empire’s
bounds, keeping their heritage and loyalty hidden lest they
incur the wrath of their neighbors. While they may have
assimilated with great distaste into the new society created
by their conquerors, they have clung tenaciously to their
former identity, albeit secretly, surreptitiously passing down
the knowledge of their lineage to each new generation so
that when the Witch-King rises again, their descendants
will stand ready to take up arms beside him and reclaim the
Men of Gog’s rightful place as masters of the world.
A Distinctive People
The Men of Gog find it difficult to conceal their heritage
because of their distinctive appearance. The pure-blooded
possess chalky white skin, dark hair, and completely lack
body hair except for what grows on their heads. Slender
and lithe, they were much taller than the First People
created after them.
Signs of Darkness: Nearly every living member of
the Gog tribe bears a marking that shows the stain of
corruption that has blighted this people for thousands of
years. The marks usually are bits of Dark Speech script
found on the skin that describe the misdeeds their soul
committed in a former life. Others might have black
blotches, strange pictures, or more traditional marks of
darkness.
Enemies of Gods
The Men of Gog pledged to purge the world of the
immortals in order to free all mortals from the cruel wheel
of life and death the faeries have condemned them to
eternally travel. They reject all gods, believing them to
be naught but jumped-up immortals who have beguiled
mortals through awe or fear into worshiping them. The
only way to break the chains binding mankind’s souls, the
Magog believe, is to destroy all false gods, tear down their
temples, and purge religion in all its forms from the world.
Those Men of Gog living within the Empire or in
neighboring nations avoid voicing their hostility to
religions, and as needed, will go through the motions of
belonging to a faith to avoid arousing suspicion. No Men of
Gog, though, would ever become willing supplicants of a
deity and thus are never priests.
Spitting in the Eye of
Father Death
People who descend from the Men of Gog realize the
inevitability of their death and what awaits them in the
afterlife. Their legacy of spitting in Father’s Death’s eye
earns them no easy fate and most face torment in Hell
rather than the oblivion of the Underworld. For this reason,
the descendants are open to anything that would extend
their lifespans or secure their souls against the horror
waiting for them.
As did their ancestors, many descendants study magic,
specifically the dark arts, to anchor their souls on Urth or
to extend their lifespans. In the Patchwork Lands and the
Kingdom of Skulls, these dabblers strive to transition from
life to death as quickly as possible to free themselves from
the anxiety they feel about dying. In more civilized areas,
such practices are not tolerated and so they must conduct
their studies in secret.
Pressure from the Cult of the New God and other
religions forces Gog’s children to hide their natures and
keep their efforts concealed. Resentment over having to
live in secret fosters hatred in some, madness in others,
and these broken people tend to be the most likely to join
nihilistic cults and secret societies who work toward the
annihilation of all things. The Brotherhood of Shadows, the
Seekers of the Wandering Star, and others include many
people of direct descent from the original Magog.
Idolized Heroes
Theologians claim all mortals have a god-shaped hole in
their minds and that people fill this hole with whatever
fits. Religion has always been part of the fabric of human
civilization, and even the Men of Gog came to venerate
Magog as a god of sorts. But they would never bend their
knees to the false gods of other humans and they remained
steadfastly opposed to any kind of devotion with one
exception.
Men of Gog idolize their heroes, whether they are
their venerated ancestors, fearless warriors, or powerful
magicians. Rather than offer up prayers or develop an
orthodoxy around these figures as do the dwarfs, the Men
of Gog recount the exploits and achievements of their
ancestors and take inspiration from them. They tell these
stories of those who came before them to fill themselves
with the courage to become something more than
themselves, and maybe be worthy someday of having their
names spoken alongside those of the Witch-King, Laughter,
Poison, the Dark Lady, and countless others.

---
27
27
The Hero’s Return
The Men of Gog’s utter defeat at the Battle of Seven
Sorrows marks the most defining moment of the Empire,
with Eronymous’s defeat of Ashrakal in single combat—
styled ever after as the great liberator slaying the worst
villain to have ever walked the world—having served to
legitimize nearly nine centuries of Kalasan rule. For the
Men of Gog, however, the death of their champion remains
a point of deep and abiding shame, one that fills them with
hopelessness and dread, since in those days they believed
Ashrakal to be Amaral reborn.
Grappling with the loss, Magog’s descendants now tell
different stories about what happened and have come to
believe in them as if they were the truth. And, who can
say what really happened nearly a thousand years ago?
Common stories involve the Witch-King escaping at the
end, or having a double take his place while he traveled to
a distant land to find the magic he needed to destroy the
invaders. Some have even said Ashrakal was not in fact
Amaral reborn, but came to prepare the way for the true
Witch-King’s rebirth. All agree, though, that a great hero
will rise again in the north to fulfill the obligation they all
have to their genie creator.
Most of these stories have certain common signs and
omens that will signal the imminent return of their
champion. The appearance of the Sword of Fire in the
night sky, the fall of the Empire, corruption exposed within
the ranks of the faithful, the rise of demagogues, war, and
the Shadow from without falling across the world. As many
of these signs have revealed themselves in recent days, the
Men of Gog have begun to make themselves ready to take
up arms and resume the struggle to free all mortals from
the yoke of the immortals once and for all.
Brotherhood of Shadows
One of the oldest cults dedicated to the Demon
Lord finds its roots in the old aristocracy of the
Witch-King’s Hegemony. A sordid society of
demon-worshipers, they ventured deeper into
darkness than did their fellows, searching the
darkness of the Void for meaning and power.
There they discovered an entity known as the
Eternal Shadow and believed this being would
give them dominion over Urth until such time
that it came forth to devour all of creation. The
Brotherhood of Shadows remains active in and
around the Empire, hatching terrible plots that
drag the world deeper into the shadow of the
Demon Lord. For more information on this cult,
see The Hunger in the Void.
Heirs of Gog
The heirs of Gog can be found throughout the lands of
Rûl, from the Desolation to the Dark Lady’s realm, and
everywhere in between. Most heirs are generally humans,
represented by mercenaries, hired killers, and other
characters found in the Shadow of the Demon Lord rulebook.
Here, you will find exceptional individuals who carry the
blood of Gog in their veins. For more characters of Gog
heritage, be sure to check out Kingdom of Skulls.
Blighter
After the fall of the Witch-King and the flight of many
Men of Gog back to the Desolation, despair gripped many
survivors. Among them were those whose disappointment
stabbed so deep that their minds snapped, seeing little
point in trying to save the world from the immortals as
their creator Magog desired. Instead, they came to believe
it was better to simply destroy it all, reducing it completely
to ash and dust. The blighters formed out of this group,
developing techniques to draw magic from the land itself to
power their dread spells of destruction.
With the Men of Gog in the old kingdom having either
become undead or slaves to the Death Lords, few remain to
stop the blighters and their insane designs. The blighters
have quietly climbed the ranks, demonstrating their merit
to their undead lords, and now lead many of the undead
armies mustering in the wastes for the coming invasion.
When freed from the shifting sands, blowing dust, and the
overweening will of the Death Lords, the blighters will then
set in motion their plans to destroy the lands of the living
and all who dwell there.
Blighters wear dusty, tattered, sun-bleached cloaks
overtop rags. They neglect their bodies, which shows in the
sores around their mouths, the fissures in their skin, and
the scabs that dot their bodies. They move about with a
shuffling gait, making it difficult to pick them out within a
crowd of undead thralls.

Occult Philosophy
Demon-Binder
The Men of Gog summoned and bound demons to great
effect, arguably practicing the art at a level far beyond
what any other peoples on Urth may have accomplished.
Having discovered and perfected the arts of Demonology
from the troll ruins, the Gog demon-binders showed little
restraint when it came to calling forth nightmares from
the Void, releasing them to devastating effect against
their enemies. The practice of binding demons fell off
considerably after the fall of the Witch-King, but their art
remains alive and well in the few enclaves that remain in
the wastes of the Desolation.
The demon-binders of Gog kept alive the ancient lore,
passing down their lore to apt pupils of great promise and
firm resolve. No matter how balanced their minds might
have been at the beginning of their apprenticeship, the
study of one of the blackest forms of magic takes its toll.
Nearly all demon-binders wear their madness openly,
their bodies bearing horrid script of the names of things
they have released from the Void, and the terrible doom
awaiting them if their souls are lucky enough to wend
their way to Hell, instead of being sucked into the eternal,
indescribable suffering of the Void.

Disciple of the Witch-King
The Witch-King’s Disciples enforced his will in the
Hegemony and ruled over the territories given to them,
some wisely but most tyrannically. The first Disciples
were those who supported the Witch-King’s rise to power
in Magog, helping him lead his great host south into the
invasion of Rûl. Whenever a Disciple died, the Witch-King
would select another worthy follower to fill the vacancy,
bestowing on them certain powers, along with an alias that
suited their talents to help conceal their true names against
targeted curse magic. Even now, the names of the Disciples
evoke terror and most believe that to speak them aloud
risks garnering their attention or, worse, summoning them.
All Disciples wielded dark magic to tremendous effect,
but also possessed some command of other traditions.
Their magical abilities reflected their adopted names,
such that Laughter was famed for using Enchantment
magic, while Destroyer had a penchant for using
Destruction magic.
The Disciples generally wore hooded robes and masks
to better guard their identities from discovery by old
family members and friends. But they were also known
to distinguish themselves and build their own legends
through their antics and exploits. By the time the Men of
Gog conquered Edene, everyone in the Hegemony knew
their names and trembled before them.
You can use the following statistics box for any disciple,
new or old. If you want to portray a specific Disciple,

Dread Cabalist
The Witch-King’s Disciples were among the most powerful
users of magic in the Hegemony, but, like their master,
each depended on a following of apprentices who formed
the Disciple’s cabal. Most cabalists perished in the fighting
and so those who claim the mantle do so without the
anointment of the Disciples who once led them. Instead,
they scour the world for secrets left by their forebears so
they can reach the same heights of magical power of their
predecessors.
Dread cabalists dwell in the vastness of the Desolation,
often found in the service of gorgons, lamias, Death Lords,
or the ancient vampire kings and queens who ruled Magog
long ago. Cabalists make themselves indispensable to
their masters, offering wisdom and council as needed and
magical support when not. When the armies of Gog march,
one can usually find a few dread cabalists flying overhead.

Occult Philosophy
Exquisite One
Many of the Gog believe the mortification of the flesh
brings clarity. Most scourge their bodies with whips and
chains, piercing their flesh and hanging weights from
hooks embedded in their skin. The Exquisite Ones take
this custom to its extreme, brutalizing their bodies such
that they live in constant, excruciating pain, finding it
difficult to sleep or, really, do much of anything. However,
the Exquisite Ones regard their self-inflicted torment as a
key to unlocking their hidden potential, to stir the demonic
spirit within them, carried in their blood since the creation
of the Hundred, in order to use its power.

---
30
Exquisite Ones have mastered the art of Demonology
and show their foul knowledge in the wreckage of their
bodies. All have abused themselves beyond recognition,
but the methods vary. Some use metal prongs to separate
the flesh or clamps to cause it to bulge in blue-black ridges.
Hooks, barbs, chains, bars, and spikes festoon their flesh,
pulling and tearing, spreading and rending them so that
the only sensation they feel is their suffering.

Occult Philosophy
Fallen
Because they were created by the great genie Magog with
demonic essence, within every Man of Gog lies the seed
of unwelcome transformation, the potential to lose their
humanity and become something other and lesser than
human. One need only look to the horde of beastmen
terrorizing the lands or the degenerate troglodytes who
boil out of the depths to see what awaits the Gog if such
a transformation takes hold. The transformation from
human into something other rarely happens overnight.
Often, it is a slow, painful process that erodes sanity in time
with the warping of flesh and soul. Those Men of Gog who
become caught in the process of transformation are known
as the Fallen, for it is believed they have lost their way by
succumbing to the shard of the demonic spirit that makes
up a part of their soul.
The Fallen retain their humanoid forms, but with obvious
signs of demonic corruption. Most will face an existence
as a beastman, with hints and signs in their features of
their futures, such as the sprouting of small horns in their
foreheads, or snout-like noses and mouths, faces covered in
patchy, bristly fur. They are usually unstable and aggressive,
tending to lash out at all around them, particularly those
who manifest no signs of bestiality. Most Fallen eventually
leave behind their people, instinctively seeking out beastmen
to live among, rising as leaders among them because of their
relatively superior intellect and abilities.

the fallen makes attack rolls and challenge rolls with 1

move up to its Speed. Once it uses Aggressive Advance,
it must wait 1 minute before it can do so again.

God-Hunter
Hatred for the immortal peoples still burns hot in the
hearts of the Men of Gog, despite the millenia since
the birth of the Hundred. Because of that portion of
them that is human and mortal, most focus on the
needs of survival. Some, however, have the original
hate of Magog burning within them, and seek nothing
but to continue their struggle against the faeries, trolls,
and other immortals. Called god-hunters, these Men
of Gog spend their lives training to prowl the sylvan
realms in search of immortal victims to kill. They have
devised certain techniques to protect themselves from
faerie witchery, easily shrugging off their charms and
piercing their glamours so that they can close in and
destroy their immortal victims with swift strokes of their
iron weapons, forged in hate and malice to make their
victims’ suffering all the more worse.
God-hunters work singly or in small teams. They cover
themselves in iron armor that grows rusty with all the
blood they have spilt, bearing many trophies from their
kills—strings of dead atomies to the severed heads of elf
lords and ladies. God-hunters have a grim cast to their
faces and an aura of horrid death, visible to any immortal,
surrounds them, striking fear in any unfortunate enough to
encounter them.

makes the roll with 2 additional boons. On a success, the
god-hunter is not charmed, frightened, or cursed.
Gog Deathseeker
The Men of Gog rely on mindless and intelligent undead
to fill the ranks of their armies, but they also encourage
many living warriors to fight fearlessly in order to earn
their undead apotheosis. Called deathseekers, they fear
nothing and fight with shocking savagery, butchering
their opponents with their axes, reveling in the blood and
slaughter. Somewhat unhinged, deathseekers adorn their
bodies with piercings, bones, mud, feathers, and tokens
taken from their victims before engaging in battle.

Reviled
The descent into corruption and madness brought on
by a serious study of Forbidden magic wreaks havoc
upon the student’s mind and body, usually leaving the
seeker of unspeakable knowledge a broken and shattered
individual. The Reviled come from those ranks of
students who receive special preparation before delving
into the Forbidden tradition’s sinister secrets, learning
how to secure their minds and safeguard their souls
from the worst of the magic’s blight. But while they can
cast those foul spells safely, they eventually become
more and more removed from the world, as if reality
itself were rejecting them.
The Reviled exist in a phase state, only partly present in
the world, drifting across the ground as they are repelled
by the land’s abhorrence to their foul nature. Most Reviled
bear several marks of darkness that contribute to their
disturbing appearance. Most cover themselves in heavy
black robes that seem to defy the elements, rarely stirring,
even in a strong wind.

Occult Philosophy
Revenants
One of the last and most successful attempts at keeping
souls from passing into the immortal-crafted afterlife came
in the form of the revenant. The first few managed to refuse
Father Death by their force of will alone. Rather than slip
away, their souls clung to the flesh and gave them a new life,
one in which they were both alive and not. The possibility
of a dead person returning as a revenant does not alone
belong to the Men of Gog, as one can find examples of
their kind throughout all of Rûl. When the Men of Gog’s
necromancers discovered this possibility, they began to
instruct whatever living they could in how to prepare their
minds for their eventual demises. Most were not able to
escape Hell’s clutches, but enough have been successful to
make revenants a noticeable number of the Men of Gog’s
surviving population.
Rules for common revenants and revenant player
characters appear in Tombs of the Desolation. Additional
revenant characters are presented below for more options.
Revenant Assassin
The Death Lords of Magog frequently dispatch revenant
assassins into the distant lands to eliminate people in
positions of power within the faiths and churches of
human communities who they believe could impede their
ultimate agenda. These assassins are bound to the sole
purpose of slaughtering anyone affiliated with the temples
or organizations of the religion specifically targeted. With
that said, the assassins make no distinction between
religions and consider anyone proselytizing a faith to be
an enemy of the Gog should they stand in the way of their
designated victims.

Revenant Knight
The dread cabalists, Death Lords, and other powerful
figures remaining within the Desolation employ revenants
as their personal guards, relying on them for their
discretion about anything they witness or overhear, but
also for their skill at arms, for all fear the machinations of
their rivals. Revenant knights earned their esteem in life,
having become accomplished warriors. That they defeated
Father Death by refusing his call makes them all the more
valuable to their masters.

Occult Philosophy
Mongrels and
Degenerates
The Men of Gog contended with physiological and
anatomical changes not long after they first entered the
Desolation. The imbued hatred from their creator Magog
for the immortals poisoned their hearts and the nascent
magic they first encountered, polluted by the Hateful
Wars between the trolls and faeries, fed upon their inner
darkness. Many showed physical signs of their corruption
in the telltale marks of darkness that afflict any who
embrace evil—but even these would only be warning signs
of the beginning of the transformations that will harass
them until the end of time itself.
Beastmen
Sources conflict about the true origins of the beastmen.
Some claim they descended from the Men of Gog,
degenerated by the foul magic they used. Others suggest
that they, along with other First Peoples, were turned into
beastmen by the faeries. A few heretics claim the beastmen
were the first aborted efforts of the genies to create humans.
All or none of these stories could be true, but, without a
doubt, certain kinds of beastmen are directly connected
to the Men of Gog. Specifically, the anubin (see Tombs
of the Desolation), those jackal-headed marauders of the
Desolation, were exiled from Gog to control what was
believed to be a malady that had broken out among their
ranks upon their exodus into the Desolation.
After being driven out, the anubin formed into large
tribes and began to prowl the edges of the Desolation’s
wastes, sometimes pressing south to harass the settlers
or to hunt fresh game, human or otherwise. The anubin
have frequently clashed with the Men of Gog, though they
have never managed to gather in numbers sufficient to be
considered a significant threat to the kingdom of Magog.
Instead, the anubin raided their settlements for slaves, food,
and supplies before melting back into the sands once more.
Although beastmen continue to live in the borderlands
north and west of the Witch-King’s former capital of
Maelfax, now called Caecras by the Kalasans, the Gog
exiles fleeing the victors’ pursuit sought whatever refuge
they could find in these untamed lands. It’s believed that
the Gog refugees swiftly surrendered to their demonic
impulses and mingled with the beastmen, breeding
offspring of more variety and horror than previously seen
in the world. Gog relics uncovered by imperial forces who
finally tamed some of these lands to found Tear suggest
some truth to these grotesque tales.
Mogs
The corruption-born trait responsible for the
transformation of many Men of Gog into beastmen also
afflicted the refugees who fled the founding of the Empire.
Fearful of returning to the Desolation, some vanished into
the hot wetlands of the Northern Reach, where they built
crude societies deep in the swamplands to escape and hide
from the retribution they feared. Generations of inbreeding
and debased behavior saw the Gog here shed their
humanity and submit to the beast within. Called mogs,
their original heritage has all but been obscured by their
resemblance to frogs. They stand twice as tall as humans,
having become bloated by their inner darkness, with moist
skin, wide mouths, and great bulging eyes.
In addition to their lost humanity, mogs have severed
all ties to civilization. They have become so reduced and
backwards that they live almost like animals. Most mog
communities, the few that exist, form around old altars
or monoliths found within the swamps, or those relics
that were dragged there. These stones have become their
gods and when night falls, they gather round them and
sing a horrid croaking song to invoke favor from whatever
monstrous deity they believe still lurks within. Some mog
communities still fashion crude shelters, but as they have
slid further and further into savagery, many simply do
without.
Mogs speak a crude, limited version of the Dark Speech,
a croaking, guttural tongue that gives them a bare means of
communicating with one another.

incarnation of their kind, one that has not slid so far into
degeneracy. These so-called “blue mogs” have bright blue
skin and smaller bodies than do their kindred, but they
are far smarter and have innate magical abilities of vital
importance to their tribes. Their hatching is immediately
recognized as a cause for great celebration among the mogs,
who will then sacrifice a great many slaves, offering up
the brains as gifts to their newborn great mog. The bands
always look to these mystics for leadership, doing whatever
they can to exalt and protect them.

Troglodytes
The darkness of Gog remains alive and well in
underground warrens all across Rûl. In these dark, noisome
places dwell the troglodytes, a race of degenerate people
whose descent is arguably claimed from the Men of Gog
who sought refuge by hiding in the depths of the earth.
Centuries of inbreeding and dark magic have transformed
them into hideous monsters who kill with merciless
abandon. Under the cover of darkness, they creep from
their lairs to murder and steal, dragging people into
their foul realms, subjecting them to unspeakable and
indescribable torments. Troglodytes receive extensive detail
in Wretched and Unclean, a Monstrous Pages supplement.
```

### Relics of the Men of Gog

**Fonte:** *Men of Gog.pdf*  
**Cobertura:** PDF pp. 35–39 — [EQUIPAMENTO]  
**Nota:** Inclui Apocalypse Cannon e as demais relíquias da seção; material de personagem posterior foi excluído.

```text
Relics
In addition to their corrupting magic that pollutes the
world to this day, the Men of Gog also left behind many
items of great power, created and imbued with the same
foul darkness that curled around the spells they cast. The
following relics might be discovered in adventures and
campaigns involving the exploration of sites tied to the
Men of Gog, or those that bring the characters face-to-face
with their descendants.
Apocalypse Cannon
After learning how to summon demons from the Void
and bind them, the Men of Gog’s demonologists began
experimenting with binding demons into objects and
freezing them into fixed forms. Forcing demons into these
forms made them more stable and easier to control, while
still being able to exploit their unique capabilities. Most
of these experiments were destroyed in the aftermath of
Gog’s defeat, but a few survived, and have become highly
sought relics.

---
36
The Men of Gog first brought out the Apocalypse Cannon
to shatter the walls of the Edene cities, the soldiers and
citizens within quailing in fear at their immense and
terrible power. When fired, the cannon released bursts of
destructive magic that could unravel anything from flesh to
stone. Strong walls evaporated after a single impact, entire
communities vanished in a single volley.
The Men of Gog built four Apocalypse Cannon. It is
believed that only one survived, and is now stored in
a vault far below the city of Caecras. Each cannon was
assembled from eighteen demons who were molded to
form the cannon’s barrel. When fired, the cannon would
drain energy from the demons and hurl it at whatever the
cannon was aimed. However, each time it was used, the
binding magic holding the demons in their collected form
weakened and risked letting them loose.
You can find out more information on these kinds of war
machines in the Shadow of the Demon Lord Freeport Companion.
APOCALYPSE CANNON
Size 2 object (war machine)
Defense 5; Health 80; Strength 0 (–10), Agility 0 (–10)
Space 4 x 4; Crew 4
Immune afflictions; attack rolls against Intellect, Will, and
Perception; attacks that can be resisted by Intellect, Will,
and Perception challenge rolls
Unstable Each time Direct Fire is used, the Apocalypse
Cannon gains 1d3 instability. It retains instability for 24
hours. See Unraveling Magic, below, for more details.
SPECIAL ATTACKS
Direct Fire (load 0, aim 1) Each member of the crew must
touch the relic and then make a Will challenge roll with 1
bane. On a failure, the crew member gains 1 Insanity. The
Cannon hurls a burst of energy into a cube of space, 4
yards on a side, within 250 yards. Everything in the area
takes 20d6 damage. A creature in the area can make
a Strength challenge roll with 3 banes, taking half the
damage on a success. Any creature incapacitated by the
damage as well as any object destroyed by the damage,
disappears, evaporating into unformed substance.
END OF THE ROUND
Unraveling Magic If the Apocalypse Cannon gained any
instability, roll a d20. If the number rolled is equal to
or less that the Apocalypse Cannon’s instability, the
object takes damage equal to its Health and disappears.
Appearing in open spaces within the space occupied by
the relic are 1 large demon, 1d3 + 1 medium demons, and
1d6 + 1 small demons. These demons are hostile to all
creatures and take the next available turn.
Black Bezoar
This small, unassuming black stone has authored more
misery than many other relics from the Gog. No one
knows from where the stone came, though some have
suggested it was coughed up by the Great Toad who lives
in the center of the world, or fell from a moonless night
sky into the Desolation, or is in fact the blackened heart of
Amaral himself. Whatever its origins, the Black Bezoar has
the power to transform a person into an undead simply by
swallowing the rock.
Undead Transformation You can use an action to swallow
the Black Bezoar. At the end of the round, you take
damage equal to your Health. The next time the light
of the setting sun falls across your body, you become
undead and heal all damage. You retain your original
appearance and make the following changes to your
statistics.
• You gain the darksight trait if you don’t have it
already.
• You become immune to damage from cold, disease,
and poison.
• You become immune to the diseased, fatigued, and
poisoned afflictions.
• You are impaired while in areas lit by sunlight.
• You are not alive and thus not subject to the effects
of deprivation.
Inevitable Decay Although you are undead, the relic does
not arrest the effects of being dead. Your body gradually
decays until you become little more than a pile of bones.
You might arrest your decay using certain ointments and
spells at the GM’s discretion.
Cloak of Dark Souls
Little is known about the Disciples who served the Witch-
King. Scraps of tales and old, usually contradictory stories
paint them as dangerous men and women, people who
were as ambitious and nearly as powerful as their master.
Legend claims that Laughter, in a bid to gain esteem with
her master, passed through the gates of Hell to liberate the
souls of her people. She crept through the foul, burning
place, snatching soul after soul, hiding them in her long,
voluminous cloak.
Laughter nearly escaped Hell unscathed, but as she was
headed toward the entrance to the mortal world, Diabolus
found her and struck her with an arrow fired from his
mighty bow. The wound would have been otherwise

---
37
37
instantly fatal, but she slipped out of Hell, and instead
bled to death wrapped in her cloak. The blood from her
wounds and the curse of the arrow bound the souls she
had stolen to her cloak, enclosing them there instead until
the cloak is destroyed.
The relic appears as a long, hooded black cloak of soft
fabric. Grimacing, weeping, and cursing faces appear on
the inner lining, and the cloak moves as if it were still alive.
Cursed Cloak If you don the cloak, you become cursed as
if by a rank 9 spell and gain 1 Corruption. While cursed in
this way, each time you complete a rest without wearing
the cloak, you must make a Strength challenge roll with 1
bane. On a failure, you gain 1d3 Insanity.
Release Shadow The souls bound to the cloak have
been corrupted by darkness and turned into shadows.
You can use an action to release a shadow from the
cloak, which appears inside an open space within short
range. When the shadow appears, make a Will attack
roll against the target’s Will. On a success, the shadow
becomes compelled. Otherwise, the shadow is hostile to
all creatures. The shadow remains free of the cloak for
1 minute or until it’s destroyed. The cloak contains nine
shadows. When the last shadow has been destroyed, the
curse is lifted and the cloak becomes an ordinary cloak
once more.
Garment of Stolen Desire
Little about the Garment of Stolen Desire has any appeal,
for it is an ugly thing, a long cloak made from the flayed
skins of nymphs, their contorted faces still twitching and
mouthing curses. A relic fashioned by a hateful follower
of Amaral, the garment bestows something of the nymphs’
magic when worn, causing the wearer to appear appealing
and desirous to anyone who sees them. The Garment
traveled with the Men of Gog into the Desolation, where
it was believed to have been lost. One tale, though, tells a
different story.
King Rothefur, who ruled in the dark years after
Amaral’s death, was believed to have donned the Garment
so he could seduce Amaral’s sister-wife. The relic’s magic
ensorcelled her as it did anyone who saw it worn; so long
as he wore the skin, she would dote on him. One day,
though, she caught him bathing without it and the magic
fell away from her mind. She entered the waters, and used
an obsidian blade to geld him. He bled out in the pool and
thereafter she ruled in his stead.
Faerie Curse When you don the Garment of Stolen Desire,
you gain 1 Corruption and become cursed as if by a rank
8 spell. While cursed in this way, all creatures who see
you when you are not wearing the Garment become
hostile to you.
Incite Affection While you are wearing the Garment of
Stolen Desire, any living and mortal creature that sees
you must make a Will challenge roll with 3 banes. A
creature becomes immune to this effect on a success,
or becomes charmed by you on a failure. The charmed
affliction persists until the creature sees you and you are
not wearing the relic.
Nymph Magic While you wear the Garment of Stolen
Desire, you gain two castings of the following
Enchantment spells and regain expended castings when
you complete a rest while wearing the relic: bewitch,
charm, compel, and implant suggestion.
Hand of Ashrakal
It is said that after Eronymous struck down Ashrakal and
raised his screaming severed head, the Witch-King’s body
dissolved into a pile of serpents that slithered away in all
directions. Some believe this was simply a metaphor of how
the Men of Gog scattered following their leader’s death and
that his body died as any other.
However, this theory remains problematic when one
considers the relic known as the Hand of Ashrakal, a severed
mummified extremity that has surfaced many times since
the Hegemony’s fall, always with disastrous results.
The Hand has always been worn as a skullcap, its fingers
spread across the crown, the palm cupped around the
back of the wearer’s head. Once in place, though, the Hand
slowly, ever so slowly, begins to clench, its bony fingers
digging into the skin until it finally pierces the skull,
granting great necromantic power that will eventually
kill its wearer unless removed by extreme magical means.
Although donning the Hand is tantamount to suicide, the
wearer can tap into its reservoirs of necromantic energy to
create and control terrifying undead slaves.
Accursed Hand You can use an action to don the Hand
of Ashrakal as a skullcap. Upon doing so, you gain 1
Corruption and become cursed as if by a rank 8 spell.
While cursed in this way, you cannot remove the relic
from your head.
Master of Undeath While you are cursed by the Hand of
Ashrakal, you can control a number of undead creatures
equal to three times your Power score (minimum 3).
When you cast a Necromancy attack spell, you make
the attack roll with 2 boons and you impose 2 banes on
rolls made to resist the spell. Finally, your Necromancy
attack spells deal 1d6 extra damage per rank of the spell
(minimum 1d6).
Empowered Undead Undead compelled by you and within
long range make attack rolls and challenge rolls with 3
boons and gain a bonus to Health equal to 3 times your
Power score (minimum +3).
A Clenched Fist The first time after you complete a rest
after becoming cursed by this relic, the GM secretly rolls
a d6 to determine the number of days that pass before
the hand begins to tighten. The effects of the tightening
depend on your stage of the curse. You begin at stage
1. At the end of this time, you must make a Strength
challenge roll with 3 banes. On a failure, you move to the
next higher stage.
• Stage 1: No effect.
• Stage 2: You take a –5 penalty to Health and you make
Intellect and Will challenge rolls with 1 bane.
• Stage 3: The penalty to your Health worsens to –10
and you gain 1d6 Insanity.
• Stage 4: The penalty to your Health worsens to –20
and you gain 1d6 Insanity.
• Stage 5: The penalty to your Health worsens to –40
and you gain 2d6 Insanity.
• Stage 6: You die, the curse is lifted, and your body
rises up 1 round later to become an animated corpse.
Iridescent Wings
of Khada-Kor
In the Desolation, the Men of Gog discovered a troll ruin
they named Khada-Kor, or “Nest of Flies” in their own foul
speech. Moving among the petrified trolls who peered at
the sun, horror etched on their faces through the gap of
upraised arms, the Gog explorers found a reeking pit in
the center of an old temple. The pit’s walls were as flesh,
puckered and veined, and gently lapping against them was
a pool of brown water, the reek so strong several of the Gog
perished from the odor. Flies, however, seemed unmoved
by the putrescence and they drank deep from the stew.
When the heartiest of the explorers stepped forward to

---
38
peer into the depths, a wrinkled demon swam up from the
opaque waters and stood upon them, waiting for the visitor
to make its wish. The man spoke and wished to fly. So the
demon snatched a fly from the air, plucked off its wings and
stretched them to human size. It then produced two long,
wicked-looking nails, each made of bone as hard and black
as obsidian, pushing the nails through the wings into the
man’s back, thus giving him what he wished most.
The Iridescent Wings of Khada-Kor found their way out of
the desert and changed hands many times, passing from
one warrior to the next, each seduced by the promise of
flight while heedless of the cost to his or her sanity. The
Wings can only be worn if hammered into the wearer’s
shoulder blades with the bone or stone nails (iron nails will
render the magic useless). Once in place, they cannot be
removed until the wearer dies.
Wicked Binding To don the wings, another creature must
nail them to your back, using nails made of bone or
stone, as iron will defeat the magic, which takes 1 minute
of work and imposes a –1 penalty per group level to
your Health score. Once nailed in place, they cannot be
removed until you die.
Creeping Madness You constantly hear the buzzing of
flies. This noise imposes 1 bane on Perception rolls that
involve listening. Furthermore, each time you complete a
rest, you must get a success on a Will challenge roll with
1 bane or gain 1 Insanity. Insanity gained from this relic
cannot be removed by spells of a rank of less than 5.
Flier You can move by flying. Outside of combat, you can
fly up to 40 miles per hour.
Obedience Skin
The Witch-King could always find uses for people, even
those who hated him. Whether by spell or relic, he could
shatter a person’s will and bend their minds toward
accomplishing any task he set for them. One of the most
infamous relics he fashioned, of which there were three,
was the Obedience Skin, a full body suit made from black
leather with openings left only for the eyes and nostrils.
Anyone placed inside the suit found themselves helpless
to refuse orders given to them by people whose souls had
been stained by darkness.
Ashrakal would put conquered nobles in the suit and
break their spirits by commanding them to perform all
manner of despicable acts. Victims found that when they
did, and served their master well, they were rewarded,
becoming more powerful and therefore more useful to
their lord and master. Thus did the Obedience Skin make
compliant servants of the Witch-King’s most outspoken
critics and opponents.
Accursed Suit When you don the Obedience Skin, you gain
1 Corruption and become cursed as if by a rank 7 spell.
If the suit is removed from you, you take a –3 penalty to
Power (minimum 0) and a –10 penalty to Health until the
curse is lifted. While you wear the suit, you are charmed
by any creature with a Corruption score of 3 or higher.
You always understand what the creature who charmed
you says, regardless of the language spoken, and strive
to obey their commands to the best of your abilities.
Rewards of Darkness While wearing the suit, you gain the
following benefits:
• A +2 bonus to Health per point of Corruption you
have.
• Immunity to the frightened affliction.
• When you take damage, you make attack rolls and
challenge rolls with 1 boon for 1 round.
Teeth of Xerexen
The mad king Xerexen ruled over the Men of Gog five
centuries before Ashrakal’s birth. Tyrannical, deranged, and
destructive—even by Gog standards—he was refused the gift
of undeath customarily given to all Gog rulers, and thus his
soul was consigned to Hell. His remains were burned on a
pyre built in the center of Magog, and the people celebrated
en masse as they watched the flames whisk his vile soul to
Hell. Once the fire burned out and the remains sifted for any
bones, twenty-three teeth were found in the ashes.
A young warlock named Zeraphon recovered the teeth
and studied them at length. He determined each tooth
was pregnant with great necromantic potential, and he
surmised that if a tooth was buried in the ground, it would
give rise to an extremely powerful undead. He tested his
theory, burying one of the blackened teeth in the sands
of the wastes outside of the Magog city. In an instant, the
sands bulged and exploded outward to reveal a horrifying
undead that promptly tore him apart and then rampaged
through the city, massacring hundreds of Gog until it was
finally destroyed.
The new Queen of the Gog ordered the teeth be gathered
and placed in a vault for safekeeping, where it is believed
they still remain.
Blackened Teeth The silky black bag contains 3d6 + 4 Teeth
of Xerexen. Each tooth is the size and shape of a normal
tooth, but is scorched. As a minor activity, you can
plant a tooth into dirt, mud, sand, gravel, or some other
material. If the tooth is fully covered, at the end of the
round, a bone machine comes spilling out from the point
where the tooth was buried. The creature is hostile to all
living creatures and takes the next available turn.
Each time you use a tooth, the magic in it is expended
and you gain 1 Corruption.
Void Star
Malice had a reputation for great cruelty. She strung up
people who displeased her and slowly flayed the skin
from their bodies, using her dread magic to both intensify
their pain and keep them alive. One of the Witch-King’s
most feared generals, in any given battle she commanded
her troops to capture as many enemies as possible, for she
was never satisfied by simply killing them. She exulted in
the prisoners’ suffering, gleefully watching as they arched
their backs in agony, tearing at themselves to be free from
her torments.
In the more or less peaceful years following the collapse
of Edene, Malice forged a great spiked mace from a fallen
star she found and filled the hollow head with unformed
substance she drew from the Void. The magic imbued in
the weapon would literally strip its victims of their form,
causing them to collapse in on themselves in horrific pain,
dissolving into a pile of liquefied, but still living flesh.
Malice vanished in the Battle for Azūl, where she and her
forces engaged the Kalasans soon after they burned their
ships, and the Void Star disappeared with her. Some claim
she fell in battle and her servants spirited her off into the
city and interred her, with her panoply, in the catacombs
beneath the city.
Enchanted Morningstar When you attack with the Void
Star, you make the attack roll with 1 boon and the attack
deals 1d6 extra damage.

---
39
39
Accursed Cruelty When you touch the Void Star, you become
cursed, as if by a rank 9 spell, and gain 1 Corruption. While
cursed in this way, you gain the following quirk: you delight
in the suffering of other people.
Strip the Form When you attack with the Void Star and
the total of your attack roll is 20 or higher, beating
the target number by 5 or more, the attack deals 3d6
extra damage. If this damage would cause a creature to
become incapacitated, you strip away its form, causing
its body to collapse into a jellied, shrieking mass. The
target heals 1 damage, becomes defenseless, and its
Defense, Perception, Speed, and attributes drop to 1. The
effect is permanent. Any living creature other than you
who can see the transformation must get a success on a
Will challenge roll or gain 1d3 Insanity.
```

## 51. Of Fire and Venom — regras, equipamentos e criaturas

### Dragons, Drakes, Customization, and Variant Stat Blocks

**Fonte:** *Of Fire and Venom.pdf*  
**Cobertura:** PDF pp. 2–8 — [CRIATURA]  
**Nota:** A cobertura termina antes do Dragonslayer master path.

```text
Scaled Threats
Dragons exist outside the natural order, disrupting
the environment, depopulating the countryside, and
poisoning the land with their foul excretions. Luckily
for the world, few dragons exist, and those who do
might spend decades lurking in their lairs before
emerging to feed.
Far more common than dragons, drakes can
be found almost anywhere, with the largest
concentrations haunting the Shield Mountains.
Drakes lack the size and prodigious hunger of their
larger kin and thus are not much more disruptive than
ordinary predators. They are cunning, though, and
in packs can equal the danger posed by full-blooded
dragons. Where dragons can live forever, drakes have
short lifespans—even shorter when they draw the ire
of a nearby community.
Venomous Origins: The jotun believe the World
Serpent encircles the planet or, according to some,
is the planet itself. From the serpent’s fangs drips
Eitr, a magical and lethal venom from which all life
sprang at the dawn of time. Pools of Eitr have collected
deep underground, having drained into the soil
through cracks in the rocks. The creative power of
this substance remains but has been corrupted by the
Demon Lord’s dread influence. Instead of mundane
creatures, the pools now birth horrid monsters that
pull themselves from the noxious stuff and find their
way to the surface to wreak havoc across a world in
which they do not belong.
While not all monsters crawl from this toxic sludge,
many terrifying things do stalk Blötland and creep
north across the Blasted Lands, finding their way into
the Patchwork Lands and beyond. The great number
of drakes and dragons found in the frozen wastes
lends some credence to the idea that these monsters
originated here, and their scaly, serpentine bodies
suggest a connection to the World Serpent.
Many and Varied: Dragons and drakes display great
variation in form. Some have four limbs, others have
two, and still others have none. Most are scaled, but
some sport tufts of hair or even fur-covered bodies.
Their coloration runs the gamut from deep vermilion
to the black of a starless night.
Despite such cosmetic variations, these monsters
all share certain characteristics. They have reptilian
bodies, resembling serpents or lizards. Nearly all can
fly, though some exceptions exist. They all possess
natural weapons, usually long teeth and razor-
sharp claws. And almost all can exhale or spit some
dangerous substance: fire, venom, or stranger things.
Finally, dragons and their kind are uniformly cruel,
wicked, and hungry.
Fearsome Aspect: Thousands of years contending
with these monstrous killing machines have
imprinted on people an instinctive fear of dragons.
Being confronted by an enormous, slavering beast
that spews fire is enough to turn anyone’s bowels to
water. But a flock of drakes winging overhead inspires
more than just fear born of survival instinct. One can
feel the malice radiating from them, their cruel intent
almost palpable in its intensity.
Keen Senses: Drakes and dragons both have
exceptional perception. Some say that dragons cannot
die of old age because they can sense when Father
Death himself comes to fetch them.
Their keen eyes are able to spot a rabbit’s movement
from several miles away. Seeing into realms beyond
human sight, they can also trace said rabbit’s path
by the heat signature of its footsteps and the spoor
it leaves behind. As well, these monsters have
unmatched hearing, making it almost impossible
to get the drop on them. Their sense of smell is also
equal to that of the best tracking dogs.
Scaly Armor: Dragons and drakes depend on their
tough scales to keep them from harm. Strong enough
to deflect the shot from a rifle, the scales are hard
to pierce. In some cases, they grow into bony ridges
that can turn sword blades and tear flesh like blades
themselves. Some ancient dragons sport sharp horns,
spikes, and flared bone plates, adding even more
weapons to their arsenal.
If a drake or dragon is killed, the strong come
from all around with huge axes and saws to spend
hours hacking through the rock-hard skin and flesh.
They might be gathering luck charms and magic
ingredients, or just proving their strength. Even
cutting up an already dead dragon is a tale worth
telling.
Hard to Kill: Even the most seasoned and skilled
warrior thinks twice before tackling a dragon. Even
if their scales are breached, dragons can take a lot
of punishment, usually outlasting any creature they
might face. Any advantage spellcasters might think
they have over a dragon is quickly negated as the
creature ignores their charms and shrugs off their
lightning. Dragons still retain a link to their magical
origins. Drakes, however, have devolved further and
lack protection from spells.
Fearsome Fliers: Despite their size, both drakes and
dragons are superb fliers, able to leap into the air and
race away with incredible speed. When hunting, they
plummet from the skies toward the target, unfurling
their wings at the last minute and snatching their prey
with their wicked fangs. Drakes might be smaller than
dragons, but their wingspan can reach almost that of
their kin, so that they are every bit as fast in a fight.
When not in combat, drakes can fly up to 60 miles per
hour, while dragons can fly up to 120 miles per hour.

---
3
Claws and Teeth and Venomous Fangs: Dragons
and drakes have a variety of natural weaponry. The
typical dragon has dagger-like claws and sword-length
teeth, each as hard as steel and ever sharp. The claws
of drakes are suited more to gripping prey, so they do
not use them in a fight. Instead, most drakes inject
their victims with a powerful toxin that attacks the
flesh, liquefying it around the wound.
Lashing Tails: Dragons and drakes have lengthy
tails to help them maneuver in the air. In the case of
the wyverns found in the cold south, the tail is a third
weapon with a poisoned stinger. Other varieties have
tails that serve as heavy clubs, spikes, or grasping
whips. Some dragons beat their tails hard against the
ground to knock over smaller foes and terrify their
enemies with the thunderous noise.
Dragon Breath: Most dragons can exhale gouts of
fire from their maws. A gland, deep in the dragon’s
chest, produces a volatile substance that ignites on
contact with air. The dragon can’t exhale fire again
until a sufficient quantity of this fluid builds up.
Dragon Torpor: Dragons are rarely encountered
because they spend much of their lives in their lairs.
Decades might pass before a dragon emerges from
its cave or grotto, and even then, it stays out only long
enough to gorge itself on whatever it can catch. Once
full, it returns to its lair and enters a torpid state as
it slowly digests the meal. The fluid that makes it
possible for the dragon to breathe fire also preserves
whatever the dragon eats and prevents decay during
this time. A dragon in torpor is not vulnerable,
though, as some fools might think. If it detects an
intruder, it can throw off its lethargy in an instant to
deal with the uninvited guests.
Unlike dragons, drakes do not enter torpor.
Instead, they hunt in a chosen region until they can
find nothing else to kill, and then fly off to find new
hunting grounds.
The Great Dragon
Mount Fear is not a natural peak. Towering hundreds
of yards above all others in the Shield Mountains,
it is in fact a borderland to a hidden kingdom of the
faeries known as Aeolia. Here, shining elves fly on
golden wings and elemental sylphs craft lightning
bolts. The elves have a haughty and imperious
outlook, and the Great Dragon, as those below call
it, is their enslaved guardian. It lies coiled beneath
Mount Fear, positioned to make sure none may
approach. An ancient dragon enhanced with faerie
magic, it is dangerous beyond belief, but like all
creatures of Fey it is intelligent and can speak, and
loves riddles. The right trick or a clever bargain
may gain its patience, or at least create a moment’s
distraction while others sneak past.
Hoards
Dragons require enormous energy to power their
colossal bodies and thus have little time for dining
niceties. They simply gulp down everything whole.
A large enough dragon will scoop up entire caravans,
whole galleys, even small trains— anything that
smells vaguely like meat winds up in its gullet. Caustic
stomach acids dissolve anything softer than rock.
Along with the blades, armor, and occasional
clockwork that are incidentally ingested are
thousands of tons of coin. These materials are
indigestible, so that gold, iron, and steel is excreted
after years of patient digesting to form the fabled
dragon’s hoard. In lean times, rather than leave their
comfortable hibernation in search of hard-to-find
prey, dragons eat their own feces. A typical hoard has
likely passed through a dragon’s colon at least twice.
A dragon’s lair is usually filled with excreta both shiny
and less so, and anyone who digs through a hoard comes
out reeking with an unrelenting stench. Dragon gold
never quite loses that smell, no matter how much you
wash it. But gold is still gold. The mad few who hunt
dragons take it as a matter of pride that no human will
come near them. Glory, they say, is measured in stink.
Customizing
Dragons and Drakes
Dragons and drakes come in a bewildering variety.
They are contrary to all nature and sense; disorder
is their only rule. Here are a few ways to alter and
enhance their already intimidating forms.
Customizing Drakes
Even the weakest dragonkin is unpredictable and
unknown. The basic drake stat block below can be
adjusted by adding new weaponry and battle tactics.
DRAKE DIFFICULTY 100
Size 1 or 2 frightening monster
Perception 17 (+7); darksight
Defense 18; Health 75; Insanity 1d3 – 1; Corruption 1d3 –1
Strength 16 (+6), Agility 13 (+3), Intellect 12 (+2), Will 14 (+4)
Speed 18; flier (swoop)
Immune damage from poison; frightened, poisoned
ATTACK OPTIONS
Fangs (melee) +6 with 1 boon (2d6 plus Poison)
Poison The target must get a success on a Strength
challenge roll with 1 bane or take 1d6 damage and
become poisoned for 1 minute. If the target is already
poisoned, it instead takes 1d6 extra damage.
SPECIAL ATTACKS
Spew Poison The drake spits venom into a 1-yard-wide,
10-yard-long line from a point it can reach. Each creature
in the area must make an Agility challenge roll. On a
failure, the creature takes 1d6 damage and by Poison (as
described above). Once the drake uses Spew Poison, it
cannot do so again for 1 round.

---
4
Acid Spewing
Drakes that deal with prey too heavy to carry away or
too hardy to easily rip to pieces might have an acidic
alternative. Their venom dissolves flesh to leave an
easy meal of bones and offal.
INCREASE DIFFICULTY BY 1 STEP
SPECIAL ATTACKS
Spit Acid The acid spewing drake spits a glob of acidic
slime at one target creature or object within medium
range. The drake makes an Agility attack roll with 1 boon
against the target’s Agility. On a success, the target
takes 2d6 damage and must get a success on a Strength
challenge roll or become poisoned for 1 minute. If the
target is already poisoned in this way, it takes 2d6 extra
damage. Once the drake uses Spit Acid, it cannot do
so again for 1 round. (This special attack replaces the

This cousin of the drake cannot fly and has only
vestigial legs, but retains the voracious appetite
common to all drakes. Instead of swooping down to
snatch livestock or unwary mortals, it slides forward

swallows everything in its path. It reaches such high
speeds by whipping its tail in a dangerous frenzy and

the Low Countries and Endless Steppe, where the tall
```

## 53. Scions of the Betrayer — regras, equipamentos e criaturas

### Darkling Weapons: Boneweave and Wyrdwood

**Fonte:** *Scions of the Betrayer.pdf*  
**Cobertura:** PDF p. 19; páginas impressas p. 17 — [EQUIPAMENTO]

```text
17
Darkling Weapons
Like all faeries, darklings recoil from objects made from iron or iron alloys
and cannot bear to handle such items, even when wearing gloves or using
some other kind of covering. Iron weapons played a considerable part in
the darklings’ defeat at the hands of the Edene: faerie weapons either broke
against the Edene’s iron shields or could not pierce their armor, while the
faeries themselves suffered great agony at the merest touch of this foul metal.
The darklings have had centuries to reflect on their defeat, particularly
upon the role iron weapons and armor played in it, and have since devised
new materials and methods to fashion arms and armor with which they can
effectively even the odds.
Boneweave
Faeries have always used bone in the creation of arms and armor, but
darklings have devised a way to make the material more resilient when used
against foes wearing and wielding iron. The ingenious use of magic from
the Necromancy tradition allows “self-healing” weapons, whose cracks and
chips fill themselves in as they occur, ensuring the weapon does not shatter
on impact with a harder material. A byproduct of this technique causes
eerie moaning sounds to emanate from the weapons when swung in battle,
an effect that works to demoralize and even terrify an opponent. Only basic
weapons, military melee weapons, and swift weapons can be made from
boneweave. They sell for the same price as ordinary weapons, but count as if
they were exotic.
Wyrdwood
More common among the elves of Alfheim and other hidden kingdoms, the
secrets of wyrdwood have found their way to darkling artisans who harvest
the material from the sacred wyrd trees found growing in old forests touched
by faerie magic. These enormous trees grow hundreds of feet tall, their bone-
white trunks up to 18 feet in diameter. So ancient and sacred are the trees
that not even the darklings dare harm them, lest they invite the wrath of the
leshys who protect them. Instead, petitioners come before the trees and lay
out the reasons for their need. If the tree accepts their arguments, the pale
bark separates and out comes the desired weapon, fully formed and ready to
serve. A tree can give such a gift only once every thirteen years, so wyrdwood
weapons are extremely rare and highly prized.
A weapon made from wyrdwood has the hardness of steel while weighing
almost nothing. They take the forms of basic weapons, military melee
weapons, or swift weapons. They are never sold, but are instead given as gifts
to worthy wielders or taken from the corpses of their former bearers. Most
wyrdwood weapons are enchanted objects.

---
```

```text
their enemies, always working against the mortals in subtle ways. Wherever
they dwell, darklings plot and connive, weaving conspiracies against their
enemies and carrying them out through the minions and agents they employ.
Darklings lack the numbers to move directly against their enemies, instead
relying on underlings to carry out their schemes. Goblins, redcaps, corrupted
fauns, changelings, and other wicked faeries often serve darklings as spies,
saboteurs, and assassins, either acting on the darklings’ orders or working

mortals, and might be found in their company or protecting the hags’ lairs.

sowing discord and despair wherever they strike, harvesting the souls of

ceaseless guerilla war against the Edene. Over time, they developed tactics
and methods that became the techniques of the manhunters. Deadly hunters,
they pick out their prey and follow them unseen, relentless in their pursuit
until they make the kill. Manhunters often wear trophies of those they slay,
keeping ears, fingers, or scalps hanging from their clothing and armor.
DARKLING MANHUNTER DIFFICULTY 50
Size 1 frightening faerie (devil)
Perception 13 (+3); shadowsight
Defense 14 (hard leather); Health 33; Insanity 1d3; Corruption 1d3 + 1
Strength 11 (+1), Agility 12 (+2), Intellect 12 (+2), Will 9 (–1)
Speed 12

resist spells with 1 boon. A creature attacking the darkling with a spell makes the
attack roll with 1 bane.
Iron Vulnerability A darkling is impaired while in contact with iron. In addition, if a
darkling touches or is touched by an object made from iron, it loses Spell Defense
for as long as it remains in contact with the object and for 1 minute afterward.
ATTACK OPTIONS
Scimitar (melee) +2 with 2 boons (1d6 + 1)
Longbow (long range) +2 with 2 boons (1d6 + 1 plus Poison)
Poison A creature must get a success on a Strength challenge roll with 1 bane or take
1d6 extra damage and become poisoned for 1 minute. While poisoned in this way,
the creature is slowed. If the target is already poisoned, it takes 2d6 extra damage.
SPECIAL ACTIONS
Choose Prey The darkling uses an action, or a triggered action on its turn, to choose
one creature it can see within medium range. The target becomes the darkling’s
prey until the darkling becomes incapacitated, the target becomes incapacitated,
or the darkling uses Choose Prey again. The darkling makes attack rolls against its
prey with 1 boon and its attacks deal 1d6 extra damage.

invisible from its prey for 1 minute or until the darkling uses an action to attack.
```

## 56. Brood of the Mother Spore — infection & criaturas

**Fonte:** *Brood of the Mother Spore.pdf*  
**Cobertura:** PDF pp. 3, 5–6. [CRIATURA] [REGRA]

**Apotheosis Spores (p. 3).** Regra de infecção independente do bloco de ancestry.

```text
Apotheosis Spores
Saprophicans reproduce by infecting living creatures
with apotheosis spores released from their bodies.
An infected creature experiences difficulty breathing,
developing a wet cough resulting from the spores
growing in its lungs and throat. In a matter of days,
the spores kill the creature, taking over its body as
described under “Parasitic Genesis.”
Transmission A creature that breathes in spores becomes
exposed. One hour later, the creature must get a success on
a Strength challenge roll with 2 banes or suffer the stage 1
effects of the apotheosis spores.
Cure Only magic of rank 3 or higher can cure this infection.
• Stage 0 The creature recovers from apotheosis spores.
• Stage 1 The creature is diseased.
• Stage 2 As stage 1, but whenever the creature uses
an action or a triggered action, the creature becomes
fatigued for 1 round.
• Stage 3 The creature’s Intellect and Will drop to 5.
It loses all professions, talents, and spells learned.
The creature becomes compelled by the spores, and
usually goes some place secret and safe to complete
the transformation. After 1d3 months, the creature
transforms into a new saprophican and retains none of
its original statistics.
Recovery Each time the diseased creature completes a
rest and is at a stage less than 3, it must make a Strength
challenge roll with 3 banes.
• 20 or more: The creature moves down one stage.
• Success: No change.
• Failure: The creature moves up one stage.
• 0 or less: The creature moves up two stages.
```

```text
Colony Guardian
Fearing discovery, and the subsequent ruin that would
result, many saprophicans patrol the lands around
the colony to steer trespassers away from discovery or,
failing that, destroy them. The task of protecting the
colony falls to the colony guardians, a small force of
capable scouts adept in woodcraft and arms. Colony
guardians develop specialized spores that help them
to befuddle humanoids who come too close so that
they can lead them away, as opposed to outright
killing them.
COLONY GUARDIAN DIFFICULTY 5
Size 1 fungus
Perception 11 (+1); shadowsight
Defense 13 (hard leather); Health 30; Insanity 0;
Corruption 0
Strength 10 (+0), Agility 11 (+1), Intellect 11 (+1), Will 12 (+2)
Speed 10
Immune damage from disease, poison; diseased, poisoned
Fire Vulnerability A saprophican takes double damage
from fire.
ATTACK OPTIONS
Spear (melee or short range) +1 with 1 boon (1d6)
Bow (long range) +1 with 1 boon (1d6)
SPECIAL ATTACKS
Psychoactive Spores The colony guardian uses an action,
or a triggered action on its turn, to release a cloud of
spores from a point in its space out into a 5-yard radius.
The spores partially obscure their area for 1 minute or
until dispersed by wind. Any creature within the radius or
that enters it must get a success on a Strength challenge
roll or become poisoned for 1 minute. Fungus and plants
are immune to this effect. While poisoned in this way,
the creature is charmed and regards saprophicans as
trusted allies and will do what they suggest. If a charmed
creature takes any damage, it removes the poisoned
affliction from itself. When a creature removes the
poisoned affliction, it remembers nothing that happened
to it for as long as it was poisoned. Once a colony
guardian uses psychoactive spores, it must wait 1 minute
before it can use them again.
```

## 57. Foulest Reptiles — lizardmen, customização & variantes

**Fonte:** *Foulest Reptiles.pdf*  
**Cobertura:** PDF pp. 3–5. [CRIATURA] [REGRA]

**Armadilhas típicas (p. 3).**

```text
Lizardmen use dart traps, poisoned needles,
concealed pits, and spear traps, but their most
commonly deployed trap is a variation of the standard
concealed spiked pit (Shadow, 203). The spikes at the
bottom of the pit are covered with sticky, semi-dried
excrement. Often this putrid coating is provided
by the lizardmen directly, but occasionally they
drop unwanted visitors into the pit and let nature
take its course over the following few days, adding
rotting bodies to the offal and poisonous blend of
bodily juices that they liberally apply to the trap’s
spiked floor. A person that falls into one of these foul
creations is often subject to infection (Shadow, 201)
or at the very least is subjected to virulent poison
(Shadow, 107) in addition to taking lethal damage.
```

**Customizing Lizardmen (pp. 3–4).** O bloco de criação de personagem lizardman foi deliberadamente omitido; ficam apenas modificações aplicáveis aos stat blocks.

```text
Customizing Lizardmen
The lizardmen have taken on a variety of different
forms and breeds over the many centuries. Some were
developed due to an evolutionary need, while others
are purported to have their roots in the capture and
crossbreeding with the native races that trespass into
their jungles and swamps.
Dart Thrower
Lizardmen sometimes use blowguns with poisoned
needles to bring down prey from a distance. One in
four lizardmen carry blowguns.
ATTACK OPTIONS
Blowgun (medium range) +1 with 1 boon (1d3 plus Poison)
Poison The target must get a success on a Strength
challenge roll or become poisoned for 1 minute.
While poisoned in this way, the target is also impaired
and slowed. If the target is already poisoned, it takes
1d6 damage from the poison.
Chameleon Hide
Some lizardmen have the ability to change the coloration
of their hides to blend in with their environments. They
tend to serve their tribes as scouts, trap-layers, and
hunters. One in ten lizardmen have this trait.
---
SPECIAL ACTION
Camouflage The lizardman can use an action to alter its
coloration to match its environment. Until the lizardman
uses an action or moves, it becomes invisible to
creatures more than 5 yards from it.
Detachable Tail
One of the more common mutations that appear in
lizardmen tribes is the ability for them to detach their
tails so that if caught, they can break free.
SPECIAL ACTION
Detach Tail If the lizardman is grabbed, it can use a
triggered action on its turn to remove the affliction by
detaching its tail. Once the lizardman uses this action,
it cannot do so again until the tail grows back, which it
does in 1d3 weeks.
Venomous Fangs
A holdover from a time when the lizardmen were
known as serpent people, these vile lizardmen can
inject creatures they bite with venom.
ATTACK OPTIONS
Venomous Fangs (melee) +4 with 1 boon (1d3 plus Poison)
Poison The target must get a success on a Strength
challenge roll or take 1d6 damage and become poisoned
for 1 minute. If the target is already poisoned, it instead
takes 1d6 extra damage.
Extra Arms
A rare few lizardmen have an extra set of arms
emerging from just behind their shoulders. These
spare limbs provide all the expected advantages,
while also making them deadlier foes.
INCREASE BY ONE DIFFICULTY STEP
Health +25
Climber
ATTACK OPTIONS
Claws (melee) +4 with 1 boon (1d6)
SPECIAL ATTACKS
Claws and Fangs The lizardman can use a triggered action
on its turn to attack with its fangs and its claws.
Variant Lizardmen
Mutation is quite common among the lizardmen and
sometimes these changes in body can result in the
emergence of a new species. Here you will find several
variations on the lizardmen.
In addition to the various lizardmen tribes, pockets
of serpent people still exist in the world, mostly in
hiding and having degenerated as well. For more
information on serpent people, see the Shadow of
the Demon Lord Freeport Companion.
Dragonman
When not reclining in the stinking mud and brackish
waters of the Bone Marsh, the ferocious dragonmen
prowl the landscape, hunting for fresh meat. These
brutish humanoids take special delight in slowly
pulling their victims apart and savoring the meat.
They eat whatever they can catch, from wildlife to
humans to even other lizardmen.
```

```text
END OF THE ROUND
Aggressive If the dragonman cannot reach a creature to

Horned Devil
The dense forests blanketing Balgrendia conceal
many strange and terrible things, from warped faeries
to skinchangers, beastmen to mad cultists. Among
the more dangerous peoples infesting the shadowed
woodland are the horned devils, a breed of lizardmen
set apart from their fellows by the many spikes jutting
from their heads and brows, multiple rows of razor-
sharp teeth, gleaming yellow eyes, and dark green
and black scales. Horned devils can also squirt blood
from their eyes to leave their enemies momentarily
blinded.
Balgrendians believe horned devils are true devils
that have escaped Hell to torment the living. Some
rural communities in this backwards province make
offerings to them, while other, madder, people exalt
them as if they were gods. Even the Cult of the New
God incorporates horned devils into their religious
imagery, presenting them as living symbols of mortal
corruption.

Indigon
A peculiar breed of lizardmen claim the coastal
wetlands in territory controlled by the Nine Cities.
Called indigons for their fine, indigo scales, they
look almost human and can pass for humans in dim
lighting. A closer look, though, reveals scales, teeth,
and slit pupils, betraying their nonhuman nature.
Any physical traits they may share with humans
have done nothing to curb their violent tendencies.
Indigons are every bit as aggressive, cruel, and
murderous as the rest of their kin. As well, all
indigons possess delicate membranes of shiny, scale-
```
