```text
Boarding Room: A single, tiny room in a boarding
home in the city of choice, there is just enough room
for a small bed and a single chest of drawers.
Large Mansion: A massive, multi-storied, multiroomed mansion either in the quiet, wealthier district
of town or in a rural area no less than a day’s march
to town. Upkeep costs include the cost of servants to
maintain the place.
Single Bedroom Home: A single story home with a
separate room just off the main living space.
Small Shack: A ramshackle wooden cube, usually
outside the city walls or in a bad neighborhood. There
is a single small bed, and a small trunk for belongings.
The upkeep costs include replacing the frequently
stolen basic belongings.
Two Story Home: This humble home can
accommodate a medium-sized family and is generally
located in a nicer part of town or with a small plot of
land outside the city. For the same cost of a singleroom home, the owner can purchase stables, barns, or
chicken coops.
Urban Manor: This large home is not quite as large
as a mansion but no less extravagant. Manor homes
are usually in the nicest developed part of town and
are big enough for a large family to live in, but they
are more commonly owned by aristocratic young
adults with no immediate family.
Yurt: An octagonal, semi-permanent, large tent.
Huge families are known to congregate in a single
yurt, but it is also the home of choice for nomadic
people or those just wishing to get away from the
bustle of city life. Yurts can be stowed and moved to
another location but must be transported via wagon.

--- PDF p. 13 ---
Owning a Business

Running a business is a great way to fund further
exploits. Characters can purchase and run a business
based on their professions. Much like dwellings,
businesses have a range of purchasing costs and are
listed by size rather than type. The GM determines
the final price of the business based on the location
of the business and the quality of business the player
intends to run. A high-quality business in a good
location will have a higher purchasing cost than a
shoddy business in a seedy neighborhood.
Each week a business will generate a profit; the
total amount of money left over after the costs of
running the business have been addressed. The
bigger the business, the better the profit. Profits must
be collected in person each week, and to do so the
owner of the business is to roll according to the profit
column on the business table. Profits from highquality businesses should be doubled.

Businesses
Size

Cost

Profit

Tiny

450 - 600 gc

1d6 cp + 1d6 ss + 1d3 gc

Small

700 - 950 gc

3d6 cp + 3d6 ss + 1d6 gc

Medium

1,050 – 2,000 gc

5d6 cp + 5d6 ss + 2d6 gc

Large

2,100 – 2,350 gc

7d6 cp + 7d6 ss + 3d6 gc

Academic Businesses: Academic businesses
include profitable teaching jobs, or consulting
services. Someone with the occult profession may
run a fortune telling business, or if they are scholars
of war they may run a school for military tactics.
Buildings include boarding schools, specialty shops,
clinics, or law offices.
Criminal Businesses: Criminal enterprises provide
a quick way to make a profit. The stakes are high,
but those cunning enough may find themselves
retiring early. Businesses can include gambling dens,
brothels, leading a group of orphaned street urchins,
assassination contracts, or even smuggling. Criminal
rackets can be run from nearly any building, and
nearly any business can be a fence. For example, an
undertaker may secretly be robbing graves.
Common Businesses: These common businesses
provide everyday goods and services: basic hospitality
services, artisan goods such as weapons and armor,
or agricultural businesses like farms or fisheries.
Buildings include farms, blacksmiths, inns, taverns,
kennels, breweries, theaters, ranches, and stores that
sell basic merchandise.
Martial Businesses: These businesses are generally
for the violent types who wish to stay on the good side
of the law. Private detectives, mercenary or military
contracting, for-profit jailing, body guarding, and
bounty hunting are all common martial businesses.

13

Most martial businesses only require an office or
barracks to run but can also include small keeps and
underground dungeons.
Wilderness Businesses: Loggers, herbalists,
gatherers, trappers, miners, and hunters all prefer
to do their business in the great outdoors. Trading
posts and goods stores are the buildings of choice to
do business on the frontier.

Wandering
Merchant Table

While out on the highways of Rûl, one might
encounter merchants or the occasional trinket
peddler traveling between cities. Traveling merchants
are often a means to acquire weapons, treasures,
relics, and other items that may not be in the next
store that the group visits. Customers of these
moving mercantiles should be prepared to pay a
50-percent markup on standard goods in areas where
the merchants do not have to set competitive prices,
unless noted otherwise. Some listings may have a
contingent of guards traveling with the merchant.
Guard listings will have a number of guards followed
by a suggested difficulty rating, listed as number of
guards / difficulty rating. The guards are generally
human mercenaries.

The pair invites customers to eat their meals

His eyes glow with the same orange breath of
a hot coal, his smile stretches between both

will try to convince a player to get into his

they will find that they have traveled into
the dimensional pocket (Shadow, page 173)
office of Rigkin, a lesser devil. His office is
made completely of black stone, down to
even the book cases and the chair the he sits
on. Massive fireplaces are set into each of
the four walls, and the heat is unbearable to
most creatures. Rigkin, from underneath a
quilt of fresh pig skins, will try and convince
the player to trade their soul for any material
possession of their choice. If they agree, they
will receive the item at that moment. If they
refuse, they may exit by jumping through one
of the fireplaces. Any player who refuses the
offer will be constantly plagued by Rigkin’s
cambion son; he will appear at the most
inopportune moments trying to convince
the player to give his bag another chance.

foul play is afoot, he will set his minotaur upon
the party. The gnome and minotaur wear
matching iron amulets imbued with magic that
extends the compel spell indefinitely. From his
inventory he sells potions relating to magic
traditions of the GM’s choosing. Quaffing one
of these potions will give the drinker access
to one spell from said tradition that the player
may choose. Access to the spell lasts 24 hours
or until the next rest, whichever comes first.
After that, the potion’s effect wears off. Each
potion costs 40 gold crowns. (Guards 0)
The merchant and his guards are actually

caravan consists of three massive wooden
containers carried on the backs of dozens
of animated corpses who have had their
legs removed. Chained to each container
are three or four human slaves who act as a
dangling carrot to the corpses. Sitting atop
each container is an orc driver. Preceding
and following the three macabre containers
are horse drawn wagons full of guards and
merchants. Players will be able to purchase
nearly any item they may need from this
troupe. Any purchased items are sold as is:
covered in blood and viscera from whatever
field they were found. Purchasing 5 or more

will result in the player gaining 1 point of

This merchant happens to be in the wrong

A gray-bearded man in spectacles skips down
the road, gleefully ignoring the crumbling
world around him. He seems to care not for
where to or from he is traveling, only that he
has just enough money to feed himself and
stay drunk. Slung across his back is a rucksack
tied to a long pole that holds a jar of beans,
a spoon, and a small library of Incantations
written in his own blood. Calculate the number
of in-game weeks that have passed in the
campaign—for each week passed the man has
one incantation. The selection of incantations
is at the discretion of the GM, but the man will
write a new one on the first day of each week.
After a player purchases their first incantation
from him, they become addicted to buying
more. Each in-game week the player must get
a success on a Will challenge roll or seek the
man out to buy a new incantation. (Guards 0)
```

## 80. An Accursed Trio — Endblade, Fate Stealer e Jester’s Cap

**Fonte:** *An Accursed Trio.pdf*  
**Cobertura:** PDF pp. 2–7. [EQUIPAMENTO] [DEPENDÊNCIA OMITIDA]

As três relíquias foram preservadas com propriedades e tabelas. Quando um resultado do Jester’s Cap manda resolver um efeito como uma spell, fica apenas a referência fornecida pela própria relíquia.

```text
Enchanted Greatsword The Endblade is a magical
greatsword forged for a Size 2 creature. When you
attack with it, Endblade grants 3 boons on the attack roll
and deals 6d6 extra damage.
Dreadful Screams Each time you attack with the Endblade,
terrible shrieks issue from it and you must get a success
on a Will challenge roll with 1 bane or gain 1 Insanity. In
addition, each creature within medium range must make
a Will challenge roll. The creature gains 1 Insanity on a
failure, or becomes immune to the Endblade’s dreadful
screams until it completes a rest.
Lifetaker When damage from the Endblade causes a living
creature to become incapacitated, the relic consumes
the target’s soul, killing it instantly. A target you kill in
this way cannot be restored to life by any means. You
also gain 1 Corruption.
Troll Blight The dark magic used to forge the Endblade
bleeds from it to blight the land all around. All natural,
ordinary plants within short range of the weapon wither
and die.
Ire of Thanatos As long as you wield the Endblade, Father
Death knows your exact location in the world. While the
relic is in your possession, you must roll two extra dice
for Fate Rolls and use the lowest result.

--- PDF p. 3 ---
Enchanted Dagger Fate Stealer is a magical dagger. When
you attack with it, the weapon grants 2 boons on the
attack roll and deals 1d6 extra damage.
Steal Fate When you deal damage to a creature with Fate
Stealer, you can use a triggered action to curse the
target. You gain 1 Corruption and the curse remains until
you use Steal Fate again, you use an action to lift the
curse while you are within short range of the target, the
target dies, or you die. The curse counts as a rank 6 spell.
While cursed in this way, whenever the target makes
an attack roll or a challenge roll, it must roll twice and
use the lower result. Meanwhile, whenever you make an
attack roll or a challenge roll, you roll twice and use the
highest result.
Devil’s Due Each time you gain Corruption from using Fate
Stealer, roll a d20. If the result is equal to or less than
your Corruption score, you become cursed, as described
above, and Fate Stealer disappears, reappearing later in
a place of the GM’s choosing.

--- PDF p. 4 ---
Jester’s Curse If you don the Jester’s Cap, you become
cursed (as by a rank 8 spell). While cursed in this way,
you cannot rid yourself of the cap. If you discard it, it
returns to your head 1d6 rounds later. In addition, you
cannot lose Insanity in any way other than by going
mad. In addition, you must use the relic at least once
between each rest. If you do not, you take a –1d6 penalty
to your Health that remains until you use it again. If you
go mad while cursed by the relic, the curse is lifted, the
relic disappears, and then it reappears somewhere of the
GM’s choosing.
Something Funny? If you suffer from the Jester’s Curse,
you can, as a minor activity, take off the cap, reach
inside, and draw something from it. You gain 1 Insanity,
but you do not become frightened from gaining Insanity
in this way. Roll 2d20 and refer to the Jester’s Cap table
to determine what emerges from the cap. Once you use
this property, you must wait at least 1 round before you
can use it again.

4

Unlucky Number If you suffer from the Jester’s Curse, roll a
d20 each time you complete a rest and note the number
rolled. This number is your unlucky number until you
complete your next rest. Whenever you roll a d20 and
your unlucky number is the result, you gain 2d6 Insanity.
```

## 81. Murder by Numbers — agentes genéricos do Correct

**Fonte:** *Murder by Numbers.pdf*  
**Cobertura:** PDF pp. 4–5. [CRIATURA] [REGRA]

Sama, Telfor e Pasus foram excluídos como NPCs nomeados. “Power Plays” foi mantido por ser orientação de customização de adversários por templates.

```text
CORRECT ASSASSIN

ATTACK OPTIONS

Assuming the Correct can ingratiate themselves to the
community, the next stage is when they are exalted by the
community. But the cult knows the road to come, and the
Correct seek out potential troublemakers early with their
assassins.
Once the Correct create a base of operations, there are
many ways to encounter the Correct. Someone might
find themselves convinced of the Correct’s teachings and
decide to become an initiate. Saving that person might be
a mission in itself where saviors might face the Correct’s
inquisitors. Infiltrators, sometimes lead by an assassin
or even one of Sama’s disciples, often carry out the cult’s
search for the community’s “disordered,” or act against
those new initiates whose demise would further advance
the Correct’s aims.

CORRECT INQUISITOR

DIFFICULTY 5

Size 1/2 or 1 human
Perception 10 (+0)
Defense 12; Health 16; Insanity 3; Corruption 1
Strength 12 (+2), Agility 12 (+2), Intellect 10 (+0), Will 9 (–1)
Speed 10
Cruel Reality The inquisitor deals 3d6 extra damage to
dazed and stunned targets.
Unraveling the Equation The inquisitor makes challenge
rolls with 1 boon.

ATTACK OPTIONS
Dagger (melee or short range) +2 with 1 boon (1d3 plus 1d6)
Whip (melee; reach) +2 with 1 boon (1d3 plus 1d6)

SPECIAL ATTACKS
Confounding Query The inquisitor can use an action to
pose a question to a creature within short range and
compel an answer from it. The inquisitor makes an
Intellect attack roll with 1 boon against the target’s
Intellect. On a success, the target becomes dazed for
1 round. On a failure, the target becomes immune to all
uses of Confounding Query until it completes a rest.

SPECIAL ACTIONS
Correct Inspiration When a member of the Correct within
short range of the inquisitor makes an attack roll or
challenge roll, the inquisitor can use a triggered action to
grant 1 boon on the triggering roll.

--- PDF p. 5 ---
CORRECT INFILTRATOR

DIFFICULTY 5

Size 1/2 or 1 human
Perception 12 (+2)
Defense 12; Health 13; Insanity 1; Corruption 1
Strength 9 (–1), Agility 12 (+2), Intellect 12 (+2), Will 10 (+0)
Speed 10
Improvised Cover The infiltrator imposes 1 bane on attack
rolls made against it for each creature it can reach that is
not the attacker.
Unraveling the Equation The infiltrator makes challenge
rolls with 1 boon.

ATTACK OPTIONS
Dagger (melee or short range) +2 with 1 boon (1d3 plus 1d6)
Sling (medium range) +2 with 1 boon (1d3 plus 1d6)

SPECIAL ACTIONS
Correct the Math When a creature the infiltrator can see
gets a success on an attack roll against the infiltrator’s
Defense, the infiltrator can reduce the total of the attack
roll by 1d6. If this reduction would turn the success into
a failure, the infiltrator gains one action and can use it
immediately. Once the infiltrator uses Correct the Math,
it must wait 1 round before it can use it again.

While many cultists are groomed toward the various
specialties of the Correct’s activities, they are often
supported, whether overtly or in the shadows, by the rankand-file of the cult.

CORRECT CULTIST

DIFFICULTY 1

Size 1/2 or 1 human

Whether on the road or amid their plans within the
settlement, the Correct is cautious and subtle. They have
no desire to enter into needless conflicts with local toughs
or meddling adventurers. The first encounter with the
Correct is nearly always pleasant and helpful. They have
been known to provide information and even support
adventurers on this quest or another. Usually, when doing
so, it’s the cult’s goal to reduce variables that may work
against its ultimate goals, but other times, such patronages
are tied to Sama’s strange revelations. No matter the case,
many adventurers find themselves supported by the cult
only to come back to its aftermath and the suspicion of the
ordeal’s survivors.

Power Plays

What precisely empowers Sama and her cultists’
capabilities? Well, that is up to you. It could be that the
Correct are just a strange cult to some unknown power. It
could be that Sama is right—or at least partially so.
In the end, it’s good to keep what powers the Correct
flexible. They’re strange people with bizarre goals—
shifting their tactics for an inflexible purpose. In later
days, the cult might pick up some magical training or start
practicing unusual religious rites falling under the sway
of other powers all toward reaching their goals. In these
cases, consider adding either magician or priest templates
(Shadow, page 265) to cult members to reflect such changes
and increase the Correct’s threat.

Perception 11 (+1)
Defense 8; Health 10; Insanity 1; Corruption 0
Strength 10 (+0), Agility 8 (-2), Intellect 11 (+1), Will 9 (–1)
Speed 10
Balancing the Equation When a cultist makes an attack
roll or challenge roll, it can make the roll with 2 boons.
If it gets a failure on the roll, it makes attack rolls and
challenge rolls with 2 banes for 1 round.

ATTACK OPTIONS
Club (melee) +0 (1d6)
```

```text
Occult Device The Apotheosis Engine is a Size 3 object
with Defense 5 and Health 100. A door opens to the
interior, which has capacity 2 and contains the controls
to operate it. If destroyed, the device explodes, dealing
20d6 damage to everything within long range of it. A
creature that would take this damage can make an Agility
challenge roll, taking half the damage on a success.
Donor Seats Four metal chairs fitted with restraints
connect to the Apotheosis Engine by thick tubes. Each
chair can hold a Size 1/2 or 1 creature. A creature seated
and restrained in one of the chairs is immobilized.
Another creature can use an action to remove the
restraints, or a creature immobilized by the restraints can
use an action to make a Strength or Agility challenge roll
with 2 banes. The creature removes the restraints and
the immobilized affliction from itself on a success.
Steal Essence If you are inside the Engine and there is at
least one creature restrained in a donor seat, you can use
an action to set the controls and flip the switch to steal
the essence from creatures restrained in this way. For
each creature, choose one of the following effects, which
take effect 1 round later:
• Reduce one of the donor creature’s attributes by 1
and increase the same attribute of yours by 1, to a
maximum of 15.
• Reduce the donor creature’s Health by 3 and increase
your Health by 3.
• Transfer the donor creature’s youth and beauty to
you. The target makes rolls in social situations with
1 bane, while you make such rolls with 1 boon. You can
choose this option multiple times to gain a maximum
of 3 boons.
• Transfer one profession or language from the donor
creature to you.
• Transfer one discovered tradition, though not any
learned spells, from the donor creature to you.
Once the transfer is complete, you gain 1 Corruption
for each donor creature, though Corruption gained in
this way is never at risk of giving you a mark of darkness.
In addition, you and each donor creature must succeed
on a Will challenge roll with 2 banes or gain 1d6 Insanity.

3

Dreadful Addiction When you successfully use the
Apotheosis Engine, you must succeed on a Will
challenge roll or become addicted to using the relic.
While addicted in this way, each time you complete a
rest without having used the Engine, you must make a
Will challenge roll with a number of banes equal to the
number of rests you have taken since last using it. On a
failure, you gain 1 Insanity. If the Insanity gain causes you
to go mad, do not roll on the Madness table. Instead, the
GM takes control of your character, who then goes out,
gets a victim, and uses the relic on that victim. Once that
is done, you regain control of your character and reduce
your Insanity total by 1d6 + your Will modifier.

Journal of
Doctor Festring

Few crimes still resonate as does the Great Northern
Massacre. This rash of brutal murders began in
Crossings, spread south into Caecras, and erupted
in several towns and villages across Old Edene. The
scope of the killings led many to think a diabolical
cult was behind them. Others swore the culprit was
a demon, pointing at the torn and twisted bodies left
behind. But when Inquisitor Xander and his cadre
of enforcers cornered the mad Doctor Festring in an
alley in the Holy City and slew him, at the cost of each
man-at-arms and the inquisitor’s arm and jaw, the
murders stopped and the Massacre became history.

--- PDF p. 4 ---

Insanity. If the Insanity gain would cause you to go mad,

Elixir of Dread Transformation The Journal includes a
recipe to brew the elixir of dread transformation. To
create the elixir, you must have an alchemist’s kit and 5
gc of special ingredients, which count as exotic items.
It takes 1 hour of work to brew the elixir and place it in
a bottle or syringe. When you consume the elixir, you
gain 1d6 + 3 Insanity at the end of the round in which
you consumed it. You do not become frightened from
gaining Insanity in this way; instead, you transform into
a monstrous brute, remaining in this form for a number
of rounds equal to your Insanity total. While in this form,
you have the following benefits and drawbacks:
• You gain the frightening trait.
• You have a +20 bonus to Health.
• You make Strength attack rolls and challenge rolls
with 2 boons.
• Your melee attacks deal 2d6 extra damage.
• You are hostile to all creatures, even other members
of your group, and you must make free attacks when
triggered.
• You must use an action each turn to attack a creature
you can reach or charge the nearest creature. If you
cannot see a creature, you can act normally.
If gaining Insanity from taking the elixir would cause
you to go mad, you do not roll on the Madness table.
Instead, when the effects of the elixir wear off, you
reduce your Insanity total by 1d6 + your Will modifier.
The elixir, however, has a permanent effect on you.
Whenever you become injured or gain Insanity, you
must get a success on a Will challenge roll with 3 banes
or become subject to the elixir’s effects as if you had

Sky Maiden's
Mantle

There was once a mortal man who gave up
everything for love. A shepherd, he spent most of
his days tending his flocks where they grazed in the
Tumbledowns, north of Old Edene. One day, he
looked up at the mountains and spied a beautiful
maiden dancing among the peaks. A sylph, her
graceful movements and her unsurpassed beauty
enchanted the young shepherd, making him feverish
with desire. He knew, though, he would never win her
heart so long as he remained bound to the earth. He
watched her each day for weeks, and his adoration of
her grew into obsession. He found he could no longer
sleep, had no appetite, and had let much of his flock
wander away.
It was in this tormented state that a tiny devil found
the young man and whispered in his ear of a way that
the shepherd might fly. He need only make his case
to the Faerie Queen. Surely she would recognize his
ardor and grant him the boon of flight that he needed.
After all, she had bestowed the gift of flight on her
love, the Robin Prince. The foolish shepherd listened
to the cunning trickster, fetched his walking stick, and
left his family, sheep, and life behind.
Northward the shepherd traveled, crossing the high
mountains, picking his way through the gloom of the
enchanted forests, over hills and across the plains,
until he found fabled Alfheim. With his prize so close,
he slipped into the queen’s throne room and watched

Staff of Ys

Ages ago, darkness found and consumed the island of
Ys, a place of ancient magic and advanced technology
populated by the mysterious Ysien. Yet the evil did not
come without warning, for wise Ygledius had a vision
of the end that would consume his people. Through
his efforts, he was able to spare most of his fellows
from ruin and seal off the island from its enemies. It
was also Ygledius who led the survivors of Ys to Rûl,
where they bargained with the emperor for refuge,
offering their counsel in return. The Ysien raised
up the Tower Arcane and set it in the skies above
Caecras, where it remains to this day, a silent sentinel
of which few have ever seen the interior.
Ygledius became the first archmage, and his efforts
to save and rehome his people earned his place in the
annals of the Empire, yet the tales told of him account
for but a portion of his work. Prior to the Ysien’s
exodus from their homeland, Ygledius had flown west
across the Nyxian Ocean in search of fabled Cadamah, the land known to occultists as the Grave of the
Gods. It is here that Tarterus sometimes draws near
Urth, so close that it sets the seas boiling, and where
things sometimes leap from the cloud-covered world
to escape its horrors.
On Cada-mah, Ygledius scoured the broken,
pitted landscape, navigating the geysers of blood
that erupted from the shattered earth and sheltering
against the corrosive rains that dissolved the flesh
of the dead titans littering the landscape to reduce
them to naked bones. Somewhere in this horrid
place, Ygledius found Graueng the Elder, an ancient
being from whom it is thought all leshies sprang. The
two fought for three days and nights until Graueng
was laid low by the power of the archmage’s magic.
Ygledius pulled free the heartwood from Graueng’s
body and used his prize to fashion the fabled Staff of
Ys, the relic that has been passed down from Ygledius
to each archmage who followed him and has come to
be known as a sign of the office.
The powers and properties ascribed to this fabled
relic have been close-held secrets of the Tower Arcane
and were only ever revealed to the trio of great
wizards who stood to claim the white mantle. The
long years of the tower floating above Caecras, along
with the infrequent appearances of the white wizard
in the city below, have only heightened the mystery
surrounding the Staff. Some claim the archmage
derives all his or her power from the implement,
while others suggest that the Staff is what holds the
Tower Arcane in the sky.
Since silence has descended over the Tower Arcane
following the emperor’s murder and the rise of King
Drudge to the Alabaster Throne, none have seen the
archmage or the Staff the master bears. With no way

Impenetrable Barrier You can use an action to spin the

Imbued Charges The Staff has 30 charges. If you are
```

## 83. The Devil's Due — Hell Tithe como procedimento do GM

**Fonte:** *The Devil's Due.pdf*  
**Cobertura:** PDF pp. 2–5. [REGRA] [GM] [REGIONAL]

Preserva o framework de abduções e todas as tabelas operacionais do Hell Tithe; esse material é de cenário, mas produz procedimentos utilizáveis pelo GM.

```text
--- PDF p. 2 ---
The Hell Tithe

At its heart, the Hell Tithe is a protection racket. As
detailed in Terrible Beauty, the Tithe is the faeries’
end of the bargain, under the threat of resuming the
ancient wars over mortal souls. Every seventh year
most communities of faeries deliver an agreed-upon
number of mortals to their infernal cousins’ wicked
claws, never to be seen again.
For all the faeries’ magic, wonderment, and
trickery, stealing away mortals is risky. Iron is ever
more plentiful in the mortal world, and every year
mortal magic and technological sophistication
grows yet more potent. Many faeries dream of a
brazen Wild Hunt to snatch their quota, but most
seek safer methods.
Mortal communities, especially in the
borderlands, are all too aware of their status
as prey for the fair folk even if they have no
understanding of why the faeries hunt them.
Thus, in the frontier are iron horseshoes hung at
doors, shrines to the Old Gods and Martyr alike
erected at crossroads, and discovered changelings
met with horror and fire.
The faeries risk their immortal lives to steal
mortals; mortals lose friends and loved ones to Hell;
the devils laugh all the while.

Stealing Lives

Devils demand as many mortals as they think they
can convince, bribe, threaten, or blackmail their
faerie cousins into providing. These negotiations
are nasty, ugly things, as even the most amoral
faerie dislikes being strong-armed by their dark kin.
For their part, the devils push to oblige the faeries
as much as possible: if they come to ruin because
the quota is too severe, or because some disaster
displaces their mortal quarry, so much the better.
Devils demand different things. Some demand raw
numbers, expecting dozens or hundreds of mortals
in their tithe. Others are more exacting, expecting
only select mortals of some vanishingly rare quality,
deep Corruption, or satisfying some fleeting whim.
No matter the particulars, the result is always
calculated to be burdensome to the faerie and
horrific to the mortal alike.

Taking Frequency
d6

Frequency

1

The faeries abduct on specific days or at specific
points during the seven-year cycle.

2

The mortal world dictates the frequency, with faeries
working in the shadows of wars, festivals, and other
events.

3

The faeries collect all their tithe at once, such as in
the seventh year at the last minute or at the midpoint
to allow them time to be choosy.

4

Tithes are collected opportunistically throughout the
cycle with no greater plan.

5

The hidden community only abducts when they must,
otherwise relying on other sources, such as their own
stable of mortals.

6

Faeries employ a hodgepodge of methods, either
due to diverse methods or division within the faerie
community.

Faerie Tactics
3d6

Tactics

3

The faeries act brazenly, out of callousness toward
mortals or desperation from infernal pressure. They
leave a trail of chaos behind their abductions and
care nothing for mortal retribution.

4–5

The faerie takers spent years, generations even, crafting
legends in advance of preying on the community to
cover their activities. Sometimes they “loan out” these
legends to other faeries for their own purposes.

6–8

The local faeries have inspired local legends by their
own actions, intentionally or not.

9–12

The faeries keep as low a profile as possible,
covering their abductions with changelings and a
wide variety of tricks and tactics.

13–15

Arrangements with local mortals or other entities
are made, such as a bandit army or group of
harvesters to acquire the tithe.

16–17

The faeries allow some devils to operate directly in
their territory on a limited, agreed-upon basis.

18

Types of Tithe-Taking
d6

Types

1

Birth Circumstance/Familial The local faeries target
one particular family; Seventhborn of Seventhborn are
given to the woods; children born on equinoxes are
given to the faeries on their tenth birthday, and so on.

2

Bargain The faeries offer up riches, favors, or other
aid in exchange for mortal lives, either the bargainmaker’s or that of others they will provide.

3

Entrapment Certain crossroads, grottos, or woods
have no exit; a hag confronts travelers and takes
any who insult her; A great lion-bodied elf lurks at
crossroads, asking riddles of passersby and dragging
away those who answer wrongly.

4

Wild Hunts The faeries ride out, taking any they may
find and spreading chaos in their wake.

5

The Wicked The faeries hunt evil mortals, criminals,
or those driven from their communities. They might
have arrangements with the mortal communities they
take from, or operate on their own warped concept
of morality.

6

The Abandoned Exiles, extra mouths, hermits, and so
on gain the faeries’ attention and these immortals ply
them with fell bargains or abduct them.

Abduction Frequency
The tithe is due every seventh year, but faeries
go about acquiring it in many ways. Rolling or
choosing from the following tables can help flesh
out a particular region or scenario.

The devils have full run of the area, having
outmaneuvered or overpowered the faeries.

--- PDF p. 3 ---
Mortal Understandings

Myths, Legends, and Tithe-Takers

2d6

Understanding

d20

2–3

Hell Tithe, down to the fate of those souls taken.

4–5

the truly wicked are taken, no matter who it is.

Hell Haunts Us Blame rests on the devils, though

A nymph (see Terrible Beauty) lurks along
riverbanks at night, inspired by a woman caught
in an affair that she saw drown her children. The
nymph appears as a wailing ghost to draw in
wayward children to steal beneath the waves.

2

An ensorcelled skinchanger hunts children and
adolescents, carrying them deep into the wilderness
where the faeries can take them. Its path is marked
by enchanted stones and local children practice
wordgames to trick it off the path.

3

A shadowy faerie prowls the community’s rooftops

4

A well-dressed changeling stalks the streets at

assumed form. It avoids the night watch, galloping

5

An elf highborn (see Terrible Beauty) has bred and
enchanted a number of local bears with shadows
and left them to lurk in abandoned buildings on the

mortals, though they devour just as many as they
retrieve.

6

Elven craftsmen trade fine furniture with the locals.
One of every few pieces is an enchanted object that
can open into the Hidden Kingdom, letting abductors
leap from beds and armoires in the dead of night.

7

A long conflict between a devil and priest left
the devil bound to a wagon wheel, its enraged

medium construct with the horrifying trait and
expert magician template). The faeries learned to
snatch mortals as they flee the terrible thing.

8

Deep within a forest whose trees house countless
trapped souls lurks a devil, permitted by the faeries
to take any mortals that wander in while it waits for
payment in children.

9

A group of 1d6 overly tall, gaunt men prowl
the countryside with wriggling sacks over their
shoulders. Whether mortal, faerie, or devil, the
locals fear them greatly.

10

A large monster made up of mismatched animal
parts and wearing a coat stitched together from
stolen children’s clothing haunts the region. It
sometimes trades its prey to the faeries, but there
are elven garments in its coat as well….

11

A team of goblins have taken up the local
waterways, bartering stolen mortal goods for elf
favors. Every month or so, they get bold enough
to try to abduct whichever mortal they currently
dislike the most.

12

An elf highborn, fond of stealing abused children to
raise as her own, relishes luring their parents to Hell
with sweetly-worded deals.

13

A local cult of devil-worshipping mortals offer up
sacrifices to their patron in exchange for faerie boons.

14

The local network of towns and cities have
a clandestine agreement: criminals and the
condemned are turned loose with a loud ringing of
the bells to be hunted by the faerie.

15

A barghest lurks in the countryside, ancient
agreements with Father Death empowering it to
harvest entire families at once should one see it.

16

A masked faerie is known to approach those cursed
for laziness and sloth, taunting and mocking them
as they rest. If they try to leave, the hunt is on.

Example Tithe-Takings

In addition to the above tables, you can roll or choose
results from the following table. Some combine
with the previous tables, while others will not. This
is intentional: the faeries are disunified at the best
of times, and you should take these examples as
inspiration for how to twist any results from the
previous tables as they please. Faeries go rogue and
splinter into factions with great frequency.
Many of these are inspired by real-world
mythologies, as there is no shortage of myths and
legends about people-stealers. If you’re looking
for additional inspiration, consider Japanese
yokai, Pacific Northwest skoocum, American UFO
abduction stories, and other boogeyman tales from
around the world.

Example

1

d20

Example

17

A pixie (see Terrible Beauty) accompanies a small
puppy through town at dusk, watching for any
who would abuse the small animal, a barghest in
disguise. At night, they hunt together.

18

When a group of harvesters moved into this
community, they quickly ran afoul of the faeries
claiming it as their own and have been press
ganged to service of the elf lords.

19

The many changelings hidden in the community
serve the faeries a few nights a year, enchanted
to aid abductions. The enchantment is unravelling,
however, leaving a few changelings free-willed.

20

A local cliff, forest, or other popular place for
suicides is haunted by an opportunistic faerie,
offering despairing mortals all manner of bargains
and boons in exchange for a new purpose.
These mortals are empowered to drag their foes,
tormentors, or others off to the faeries or straight
to Hell itself.

Running the Tithe
Most Hell Tithe scenarios where the characters are
cast as mortals feature the faeries in an antagonistic
role. Hell counts few allies in the realm of mortals, and
opposing the hunting and harvesting can unite even the
most disparate factions. Many of the faeries that carry
out the Tithe-Taking are just as monstrous as their devil
kin, after all. There are plenty of mortal foes in such a
story, too, as clandestine faerie pacts can empower those
willing to forsake their fellow mortals to the fires of Hell.

Mortal Plot Hooks
d6

Hook

1

The characters must saddle up and race after elf
or devil riders in the night to save the children
they’ve stolen away in sacks.

2

Helpful faeries, fond of the characters, warn them
that the wild hunt is coming.

3

A familiar path twists and turns, the characters
stumble into a faerie’s trap, and they must escape
before the fair folk come for them.

4

One character’s loved one is revealed as a
changeling knowledgeable of the Hell Tithe, and
the characters must find a way to rescue the
original in time.

5

6

A phantom haunts the community, hurling
accusations at people it claims led to its death in a
failed elf abduction.
One of the character’s antagonists refuses to stay
dead, and a devil or faerie suggests a more final
method, for a price....

Faerie characters may be pressed into service for
gathering up mortals by their lords as an individual
task for a session’s adventure, or the players could take
the role of dedicated mortal-takers. Such campaigns
can lead to an interesting reversal of perspective,
a chance to play the lurking monster rather than
the frightened victim. It might explore the toxic
relationship between faeries and devils, including
intense negotiations, subterfuge, and scheming as
both kin try to outmaneuver each other.

Listening to your Table
Be mindful of your players’ comfort levels. The
thought of being abducted or having your child
stolen away with malicious intent is one of the
greatest horrors imaginable, and sadly all too
common in the real world. The Hell Tithe, for all
its supernatural elements, boils down to slavery
and human trafficking, and participating in that
simply isn’t many people’s idea of fun escapism.
Find other wrinkles if you wish to have your
games feature or focus on the Hell Tithe, such as
focusing on the wicked souls to be sent to Hell,
stopping the tithe-takers, or seeking revenge on
the faerie or devil alike.

Even those faeries who come to find a twisted joy
in the hunting of mortals or the cleverest of traps can
never forget that they are doing so to benefit Hell, not
themselves. Sneering devils make for good antagonists
in such a campaign, and every faerie dreams of finding
power or leverage enough to declare independence
from the Hell Tithe. Every faerie character in such a
story is likely to be looking for ways to subvert the Hell
Tithe, to give the devils as little as possible, or avoid
staining themselves with Corruption.

Faerie Plot Hooks
d6

Hook

1

A devil’s been caught poaching mortals. The
characters are called on to bring them in for their
lords to leverage the violation against Hell.

2

The fall of the Empire has left the local imperial
garrisons a mess, and the orc commander’s posted
a bounty for deserter heads... but she might
be willing to accept other proof as long as the
despoiling stops.

3

A rival hidden kingdom claims the character’s
territory, forcing conflict in court or by arms.

4

A demonic cult threatens to destroy the faerie’s
mortal hunting grounds.

5

A reckless band of elves raided the wrong mortals,
and the characters are caught in the storm as both
sides go to war.

6

Hell demands one extremely dangerous individual
be claimed; in exchange, the tithe is called off for
the cycle.

Another way to incorporate the Hell Tithe into a
campaign is to have all the players play changelings.
They could be “left overs” from the last seventh year
or entirely incidental abductions to the Hell Tithe.
The changelings can fit easily into either of the
previous categories; they can side with their mortal
surrogates against their faerie sires, or act as agents for
the hidden kingdoms. They can also pursue their own
agenda, but whatever they choose, a campaign where
every character can masquerade as someone else is
sure to be filled with intrigue and clever ploys.

--- PDF p. 5 ---
High Plains Drifter or books like Devil’s Rose, where
the characters act as agents of Hell after corrupt
mortals or escaped wraiths. See Exquisite Agony for
the cambion ancestry and many suitable character
options, and Between Two Worlds for the Hellion
expert path. However, Hell enlists anyone willing to
do its dread work and is only too happy to stain such
servants with corruption.

Hellish Plot Hooks

Changeling Plot Hooks
d6

Hook

1

Despite their secret nature, the changelings have
thrown in their lot with their mortal communities
and seek to drive away any further tithe-taking.

2

3

4

5

6

Finally, you can pitch the idea of having the
```

```text
Joining the Compact

The Compact is always looking for new agents,
especially those with unusual skills and abilities
who could be of service to the organization’s larger
objectives. For this reason, the characters might attract
the Compact’s attention and become Candles or
even fully employed Agents, depending on how they
acquit themselves on assigned missions. Characters
who serve the Compact as Candles might be called
to provide information to their handlers or carry
out certain tasks. Once they prove themselves useful
over the course of several assignments, Candles are
sometimes invited to become Agents. Those who do
will receive a modest stipend enabling them to afford
a comfortable lifestyle and whatever materials they
might need to complete their missions.
Characters belonging to the Compact might benefit
from taking the Agent expert path described in
Kingdom of God.
```

```text
Madness of the Machine God

From each house to the next, it would seem whoever
lived there simply decided to leave, abandoning all
their worldly possessions. But one house in particular
is different: the door stands ajar, cupboards have been
swept bare of food save an overlooked moldy piece
of cheese or heel of bread. A safe that once guarded
precious or personal treasure sits open and the
wardrobe is vacant. Though the rest of the community is
oppressively silent and the evidence frustratingly scant,
this house has a secret to tell. Its master or mistress left
in a hurry.
A nearby village five or ten miles off might tell a
different story. Perhaps the fleeing homeowner reached
it, warned the residents, and was believed and taken
in. In such a place, one might have the opportunity to
meet with the eyewitness who fled. However, visitors
might encounter suspicious and wary villagers in
arms, who either refuse entrance or subject them
to inexplicable prodding and poking like the most
bellicose security guards.
But then, there is every chance the witness never made
it, or chose to flee into the wilderness, thinking it safer
sanctuary than another settlement. The next town might
be as quiet and bereft as the first, or it might tell a darker,
more brutal story.
In such a village, there is evidence of a fight. Homes
have been burned to the ground, dirt lanes and gardens
reduced to trampled mud. Things lie scattered about
like so much broken trash. Doors are ripped from lintels
and posts, furniture is smashed to kindling, and grisly

5

Wherever the Machine God goes, madness
follows. Spreading like a foul disease, the
Machine God’s influence bleeds into its environs,
about a quarter-mile at the end of each hour
it remains immobile, to a maximum radius of 5
miles. Whenever a creature within the area of
the Machine God’s influence completes a rest, it
must get a success on a Will challenge roll or gain
1d6 Insanity. Rather than becoming frightened
from gaining Insanity in this way, the creature
becomes fixated on its physical flaws or those it
perceives in others around them. If the creature
goes mad from gaining Insanity in this way, it
does not roll on the Madness table. Instead, it
becomes compelled and uses its action to make
“modifications” to the offending physical trait
using whatever means happen to be at hand—a
knife, a jagged piece of glass, a pair of rusty pliers.
The compelled affliction remains until the grisly
modification is complete, resulting in horrifying
mutilations, maiming, or death, unless the
compelled creature is restrained in some way or
rendered unconscious.
The Machine God typically remains in place for
2d3 days before it moves on, scrabbling away until
it vanishes altogether to reappear somewhere else
in the world.

Tracking the Horror
The caravan is difficult to follow, not only because
the tracks are muddled and incoherent, what with so
many hands and feet of varying description jerking
and pulling it along, but also because after a spree of
attacking and subduing a string of little towns, it seems
to disappear for weeks or months at a time. It sequesters
itself in dark, secluded forests and the shadows of
ominous mountain ranges to replenish its forces or
repair its fleshy mount. But eventually, persistent
characters might find what they’re looking for.

The Macabre Wagon
Once located, the caravan is much as it has been
described: a large, seemingly mundane covered wagon,
though it lacks horses to draw it or teamsters to drive it.

--- PDF p. 6 ---
Carrion birds wheel through the sky overhead, diving
from time to time to pick at the vehicle’s exterior before
rising once more, making their displeasure known
through caws and screeches.
A curious odor wafts from the wagon, growing
stronger the closer one gets: a reek redolent of
unwholesome meat still covered in hair, burning in some
infernal forge, fouling the air all around. When visitors
draw even nearer, they see what forms the covering
over the wagon’s bed—a multitude of faces patched
together with weeping crimson stitches, lashes in place
over empty eye sockets and mouths gaping. Where
bonnet meets bed, arms and shoulders once belonging
to children grasp perpetually at the empty air, with the
blind instinct to ensnare. The whole of it is supported by
dismembered arms and legs rather than wheels, fingers
and toes digging into the ground for purchase, straining
beneath a weight that would be too great to bear without
help from the multitude of evident victims who work in
concert to lift its unwieldy bulk.

AVATAR OF THE MACHINE GODDIFFICULTY 1,000

Attacking the Wagon

ATTACK OPTIONS

The Machine God defends itself from attacks by
transforming the wagon into a gigantic monstrosity.
Enormous appendages, each a horrid fusion of
machinery and flesh, lift the vehicle up, revealing
a frowning face, a grotesque mask fringed with the
reaching and clawing arms and hands that sprout from
its sides. In this form, the Machine God fights for a few
rounds before teleporting away.

The Flesh Forge
Rather than attack the wagon, the player characters
might think to peer inside, looking through the flaps
at its back. If so, they see the interior of a space far
larger than what the wagon could possibly hold, room
enough for a dozen clockworks to stand at processing
stations in front of a roaring oven. Room enough for
them to rip limbs from bodies, eviscerate the remains,
and chuck discarded organs into the gaping maw of an
engine powered by flesh. Room enough for metalwork
to construct the gears that power bronze and copper
bodies once a soul has been ripped from the afterlife.
Room enough for cages holding hopeless, helpless living
mortals who await their turns for processing.
While nothing about this ambling monstrosity evokes
anything less than horrific despair, something else,
above all, resonates within its recesses. This is what
cows the captives within, robbing them of the ability to
scream or attempt escape: a pair of wide-set, monstrous
brown eyes above the organ-powered oven. They bulge
from the interior walls, bloodshot and wild as fire dances
across them. They blink slowly, but never fully close.
They watch all that happens and never sleep. When a
batch of viscera is tossed into the oven, they roll back
till the only color left is sickly white run through with
lightning bolts of red. Whether in pleasure or disgust is
impossible to discern.

dealt by the avatar’s appendage attack is absorbed into
the avatar’s body, causing the avatar to heal damage
equal to the target creature’s Health score.
Stomp (melee) +8 with 3 boons (4d6 + 6 damage plus
Crushing Step)
Crushing Step A target creature falls prone and becomes
immobilized until the avatar moves or makes a stomp
attack. A creature immobilized in this way is blinded,
cannot stand up, and has total cover while it is trapped
under the avatar’s foot. At the end of each round the
creature is immobilized in this way, it takes 6d6 damage.
A creature immobilized in this way can use an action
to make a Strength attack roll with 2 banes against the
avatar’s Strength. On a success, the creature removes the
immobilized affliction from itself and crawls 1 yard out
from under the avatar’s foot.

Double Attack The avatar makes two appendage attacks. It
can make a stomp attack in place of one of these attacks.
Moan of the Machine God The avatar’s mouth yawns wide
and emits a low, mournful moan that spreads out from a
point in its space into a 20-yard radius. Each creature in
the area that can hear the moan must get a success on a
Will challenge roll with 3 banes or gain 1d6 Insanity. Once
the avatar uses Moan of the Machine God, it must wait
1d3 rounds before it can use it again.

SPECIAL ACTIONS
Teleport The avatar teleports to a point in the world that it
chooses anywhere within 10d20 + 200 miles.

Epic Recovery The avatar removes one affliction from itself.

up in open spaces within its reach. These clockworks
can take the next available action. Once the avatar
uses Spawn Horrid Clockwork, it cannot do so again
until all the previous clockworks it has spawned are
incapacitated.

to take notice and dismantle its body.

The Maddening Maze
Two yawning alcoves flank the machinery at the far
side of the chamber and lead into a maze of passages
manifested by the Machine God’s horrid imaginings.
Each passageway leads to more corridors, stairways, and
chambers, some connecting to hidden rooms that hold
dreadful truths and terrible dangers. The arrangement
of these spaces changes with the thoughts of the
Machine God who waits somewhere within, making the
entirety of the labyrinth impossible to navigate.

Challenges

The maze has no fixed form. Characters might venture
down one corridor or climb up a staircase and then
turn back the way they came, only to find themselves
in an utterly unfamiliar environment. For this reason,
tracking the group’s progress uses an abstract method.
As characters explore the maze, they have opportunities
to gain revelations into the nature of the being. On
attaining the eighth revelation, they stumble into the
Heart of the Machine God, which is described below.
Opportunities for revelations result from rolls on the
following tables. Simply roll on the first table and then
consult the appropriate table for that encounter. After
the group successfully deals with the encounter, they
receive one revelation.
Revelations can take the forms of clues, such as
“Turn right at the next intersection”; clockwork keys
to open doors blocking the path; or lenses that, when
worn over the eyes, reveal glowing footprints on the
floor, hidden openings, or a ghostly hand that guides
the group for a time.

maze, they hear murmuring voices emanating from the
walls, whispers that promise all manner of wild things:
incredible knowledge, astounding power, and the ability
to cheat death itself. After the group contends with a
maze encounter, roll 1d6 and multiply by 10 to determine
how many minutes pass before they come to something
else of interest. For every 30 minutes spent in the maze,
have each member make a Will challenge roll with 1
bane to avoid gaining 1 Insanity from the constant hum
of voices.

a character falls 11 or 22 yards, depending on the
number of successes gained so far. Each time a

the grinding of the wall. The characters find the

gaining Insanity in this way, the character with
the most damage discovers a revelation hidden

A crypt is filled with broken clockwork pieces,

A chamber 30-yards wide and long has a door

her reflection, the corpse of the last is revealed to
be carrying a revelation.

The characters enter a large, gloomy chamber in
the center of which floats a mechanical heart. If
the characters attack the heart, it unfolds into a
humanoid shape and fights back (as a golem).
Destroying it reveals a revelation.

Heart of the Machine God
Once the characters collect the eighth revelation, the
path to the central chamber opens to them, where
they find a room with nothing in it but a small,
shriveled human heart, suspended at the center of a
dais surrounded by cold, unyielding walls. From its
ventricles and atriums, threads of arteries reach from
the ceiling to the floor, holding it in place as it pulses
with infernal darkness. This is all that remains of the
Machine God: the young optimist turned madman,
turned Horologist, turned abomination, whose
children and followers have so perverted his original
vision that he is unrecognizable as anything other than
a roving monster.
The heart counts as an object with Defense 5 and
Health 100. Each time the characters deal damage to
the heart, it releases a psychic screech, forcing each
creature in the chamber to make a Will challenge roll
with 3 banes. On a failure, the character gains 1d6
Insanity. In addition, a promethean with Defense 20
and Health 200, whose body incorporates mechanical
upgrades, forms in the fleshy wall coverings, tears
free, and attacks the group. Each time the heart takes
damage after the first, the promethean either heals
1d20 damage or can immediately take an extra turn
beyond the normal restriction. If the characters destroy
the promethean, the heart takes 5d20 damage.
```

## 86. Black Sun Dawn — Manuscript, criaturas e enchanted objects

**Fonte:** *Black Sun Dawn.pdf*  
**Cobertura:** PDF pp. 2, 7–9 e 11–17. [EQUIPAMENTO] [CRIATURA] [REGRA] [DEPENDÊNCIA OMITIDA]

Rathran Crux e Crux Matron foram excluídos como NPCs únicos nomeados. Foram mantidos todos os adversários genéricos, os nomes de spells presentes em stat blocks e as propriedades alternativas de enchanted objects.

```text
BLACK SUN MANUSCRIPT
The Black Sun Manuscript has a long and sordid history,
one filled with disaster and defeat for everyone who has
come into its possession. Although many copies exist, only
the original book has power. The book measures three feet
by two feet and is a foot thick.
The book is written in High Archaic in a scrawling hand
punctuated by woodcut prints depicting awful beings
that defy description along with hand-drawn diagrams
surrounded by notes and corrections. Although much of
the ink is black, sections appear to have been written in
blood. It takes 240 hours of reading and study to consume
the book’s full contents and only then can one apprehend
its power and can access the book’s properties. You gain
3 Corruption when you finish reading the book.
Dread Secrets You make challenge rolls to recall
information concerning taboo subjects, the occult,
and magic with 3 boons.
Magic of the Black Sun You discover the Forbidden,
Madness, and Time traditions. You do not gain
Corruption for discovering the dark magic traditions.
The Madness tradition appears in Occult Philosophy.
If you don’t have access to it, you can use a different
tradition in place of Madness.
Call the Elder Gods You can perform a ritual included
inside the book. To perform the ritual, you must
concentrate for 1 hour, during which time you inscribe
a complex diagram on a flat surface you can reach using
rare inks and ingredients worth 1 gc. When you finish,
you must expend the casting of a spell. The rank of the
spell whose casting you expended determines what
appears: 2 or less produces a small monster, 3 produces
a medium monster, 4 produces a large monster, and
5 or higher produces a huge monster. The monster has
the horrifying and flier traits, and it obeys commands
you give it in High Archaic. The monster remains until it
is destroyed. Each time you perform this ritual, you must
get a success on a Will challenge roll with 3 banes or
gain 1d3 Insanity.

By day, the lands around the Occlusion are empty,
the wreckage of the terrain left in ruin by some
forgotten calamity. By night, the blasted expanse
comes to life, when the misbegotten crawl out
from the rocks, from beneath the shelves, and out
of the pits pocking the surface, liberated by the
sun’s departure and ready to feed their vile appetites
for food and pleasure.
The misbegotten are a breed of monster created
by the cabalists’ failed experiments. Cast out from
the Occlusion, the misbegotten must make do in the
wild. Formed from human stock, the misbegotten still
show some signs of their heritage, being humanoid in
shape, but always marked in some way or another by
the horrors inflicted on them. Abraded flesh, hideous
scars, extra appendages, misshapen features, and
worse beset them, but in no way diminishes their
hunger or their desire to copulate.
The misbegotten range far from the Occlusion
each night, scouring the lands for anything they
might eat or fuck. Often, they fall on their victims,
devouring them and violating their corpses, spilling
their purplish seed into wounds left by their claws
and teeth. When forced to go without, they howl in
fury and turn on each other in an orgy of violence. In
no danger of running out of their kind, such is their
fecundity, the appalling slaughter serves to keep their
numbers in check.

The cabalists had begun to extract strange lampreylike creatures through tiny portals torn open to the edges
of the universe. The creatures showed intelligence and
a capacity for working magic, but they could not find a
way to communicate with them. The gift of thirty dwarf
prisoners, offered them a possible solution.
The cabalists drained the hoods of their vital fluids
and removed the backs of their heads, including
their brains. They then pumped the bodies with an
alchemical fluid and attached a glass container, filled
with the same fluid and the weird parasites, to their
heads. This new arrangement allowed the parasites
to control the bodies and reveal their secrets to their
summoners, speaking in High Archaic.
Alien Intellect: The entities, called ageet, drawn
from the edges of the universe, were spawned from
the heaving bulk of a dead god set adrift in the darkest
reaches of space. Each ageet possesses a fragment
of the being’s intellect and command over darkness.
They are keenly interested in their adopted world
and have become willing accomplices in the Cabal’s
insidious work. Ageet consider themselves partners
with the Cabal, rather than their servants. One day,
they might grow powerful enough to branch out on
their own and pursue their own agenda.

Murderous Spies

Hoods undertake missions involving intelligence
gathering, sabotage, murder, and mayhem. They
use Shadow magic to cover their movements and to
enter places normally forbidden to them. The Cabal

chooses targets, using numerological formulas to
predict which individuals and places might frustrate
their efforts to prepare the world for the coming
darkness and the hoods carry out the task without
hesitation or complaint. When on missions, hoods
work in small numbers, no more than three. If they
need additional muscle, they recruit cultists from the
field and consider them expendable.

Megpee

The Cabal of the Black Sun has eyes and ears
everywhere, trusting the work of gathering
information to the megpees, who ensure that other
agents in the field carry out their missions. These
strange bird constructs have the bodies of ravens with
the heads of porcelain dolls, whose black eyes swivel
in their heads and who speak without ever moving
their cold lips. Megpees accompany hoods and
cultists at work, recording everything they witness so
they can give a full accounting to their masters when
they wing their way back to the Occlusion. When not
on a mission, the megpees sometimes gather in flocks
atop the battlements or wheel in the sky overhead,
diving at travelers to get a good look at those who will
soon grace the dungeon depths below the Occlusion.

13

--- PDF p. 14 ---

Talons (melee) +4 with 1 boon (1d6)

SPECIAL ATTACKS
Compelling Direction The megpee uses an action, or a
triggered action on its turn, to reach into the mind of
one creature it can see within long range and makes
an Intellect attack roll against the target’s Will. On a
success, the megpee moves the target up to half its
Speed in a manner it can normally move. The movement
does not trigger free attacks.
Destructive Chime The megpee makes a chiming noise
that causes a wave of force to spread out from a point
in its space out to a 5-yard radius. Each creature in
the area other than the megpee must make a Strength
challenge roll with 1 bane. A creature takes 5d6 damage
and becomes stunned for 1 round on a failure, or just
takes half the damage on a success. Once the megpee
uses Destructive Chime, it must wait 1 minute before it
can use it again.

14

Messengers of the Black Sun
The disciples sometimes dispatch a megpee to treat
with a particularly difficult and dangerous adversary.
The megpee is empowered to bargain on behalf of the
Cabal, though within limits, and so in this capacity,
the megpee might make all kinds of offers in order to
tempt their foes from continuing their efforts against
the Cabal. Clever, megpees conduct these meetings
from a distance, usually perched somewhere they can
be heard but out of their opponent’s reach.

Scran

Tunnels riddle the ground beneath the Occlusion.
These lightless corridors collect the filth and offal
that drain from the encrusted chutes and pipes
that carry the effluvia from the crooked chambers
above. Where these jagged tubes jut from the walls,
those wandering the depths are bound to find scran
suckling upon them, engorging themselves of the foul
nectar spawned from the countless horrors infesting
this blight on the world.
Scran are among the rare few monsters
created by the Cabal that have managed
to perpetuate themselves and thus
escape from the Occlusion to ensconce
themselves elsewhere in the Patchwork
Lands. Scran have bodies of worms, their
rubbery flesh maggot-white and bristling
with keratin horns. Human heads with
slick faces contorted into grimaces of
pain and horror extend out from the
front of their bodies, while their tails
terminate in puckered sphincters from
which issues a sweet-smelling, thin,
yellowish slime.
Although bred from humans, they
retain none of the higher thought or
intelligence of their ancestors. Instead,
the fulfilment of their basic needs defines
their existence. They slither through the
noisome dark in search of food, water,
and suitable mates. Some gather into
colonies of modest size, though such
gatherings typically serve to protect a
clutch of eggs, each a black, hard shell
encasing a noxious stew and embryo.
Scran moan, chuff, and make other
noises, but they never speak.

Attach When a scran gets a success on an attack roll it

concentrate on this effect, the target to which it is

success. Whether the roll results in a success or failure,
the creature to which the scran was attached takes 1d6
damage from having its body torn by the scran’s teeth.

Maggot Infestation
The Cabal has never taken an interest in the scran and
their lack of action permits the scran to move freely
below the Occlusion and, in some case, away from the
Cabal’s area of influence. In recent years, many of the
petty rulers of the Patchwork Lands have complained
of scran infestations growing beneath their ramshackle
castles and keeps. Most of these minor rulers have
turned to mercenaries and adventurers to clear out the
infestation lest their numbers grow out of control. Scran
lay dozens of eggs, which hatch in a matter of days.

Tatterdemalion

Maintaining the Occlusion falls to a wretched breed
of constructs assembled from discarded body parts
and other materials and to which the disciples bind
the spirits of their enemies, starting with the students
they murdered in Lij. Tatterdemalions appear as
misshapen dwarfs, all twisted up and broken, and
they cover themselves in whatever scraps of material
they can find. They cringe away from threatening
creatures, but can muster up courage when cornered,
becoming vicious fighters. Even though the spirits
bound to them are unwilling victims of the Cabal’s
magic, each has been imbued with an overriding
sense of self-preservation to prevent them from
simply committing suicide.

ATTACK OPTIONS
Improvised Weapon (melee) +2 with 1 bane (1d3)

END OF THE ROUND
Flee! If the tatterdemalion is frightened, it moves up to
half its Speed away from the source of its fear without
triggering free attacks.

Tatterdemalions speak haltingly in the Common
Tongue, frequently misusing words, revealing the
disorder of their minds.

Unlikely Ally

Freeing a spirit from a tatterdemalion could give the
player characters a useful ally, provided they can
somehow communicate with it and convince it to aid
them in their fight against the Cabal. These spirits
have no reason to love their tormentors and so might
divulge certain secrets that would be of use to those
who would end their dark tyranny.

Black Sun Disciples

The Black Sun Manuscript’s reputation lures the mad
and the wicked into scouring the lands for it, to
uncover this most unholy tome and learn its secrets.
The Cabal of the Black Sun quietly encourages
outsiders to seek out the book and even circulates
forgeries containing a few tantalizing truths to draw
these outsiders into their fold and make them witting
or unwitting servants of the Cabal’s designs. As their
numbers grow and spread, so too does the Cabal’s
network of minions.
A typical cult of the Black Sun grows up around
one or two leaders who have come into possession
of fragments from the book, a copy, or one of the
forgeries. Upon studying the writings, the leaders
come to see Rathran Crux as their prophet and
guide. Some cults even go so far as to worship him,
offering prayers and sacrifices to his name. The
leaders gather likeminded individuals, preying on
the weak and the fragile and drawing them in with

15

--- PDF p. 16 ---
promises of vengeance, power, or whatever else they
could desire. These cultists never learn the full truth
of what their leaders have discovered—which is in
itself little compared to the knowledge amassed by
the Cabalists—to ensure these disciples never balk
at the Black Sun’s ultimate aim and betray them to
their enemies.
Black Sun disciples pursue their own agendas.
They study dark magic, seek out relics left behind
by the Men of Gog, and kidnap innocents for ritual
sacrifices in the hopes of gaining the Black Sun’s
attention. Disciples who have shown themselves to
be resourceful and competent might earn attention
from a megpee, who then makes use of them for
its masters. These disciples accompany hoods on
missions or might be sacrificed as a distraction while
other agents move in to secure objects that the Cabal
would have for themselves.
Like the Cabalists, self-mutilation preoccupies
cult members and most sport signs of their debased
interests. When gathering for unholy ceremonies,
they don gray robes with pointed hoods that conceal
all but their eyes, over which is painted the black sun.

Treasures of the Cabal

In addition to sculpting creatures and reaching
across vast distances to pluck alien entities from the
furthest reaches of the universe, the Cabalists have
also created many strange devices to aid them in
their work. Although these items most likely reside
in the Occlusion, some might have found their way
elsewhere, likely corrupting whomever happens to
find them.
The Cabalists often create magical objects in
order to help them in their work, but many times
their efforts fail and result in oddities with strange
properties. Enchanted objects originating with the
Cabal are made from metal, usually bronze, fashioned
to look like horns, teeth, organs, and other organic
body parts, or collections of those parts. Others
resemble machines with clockwork components,
hoses, flashing lights, and other mechanical
components.
When rolling to determine the enchanted object’s
properties, you can use the tables presented in
Shadow (see page 208) or you can use the following
table instead.
```

## 87. Demon Lord Errata — correções com precedência

**Fontes:** *Demon Lord Errata (19nov17).pdf* e *Demon Lord Errata (10oct17).pdf*.  
**Cobertura:** PDFs pp. 1–3; somente correções dentro do escopo. [BASE] [EQUIPAMENTO] [CRIATURA] [REGRA]

**Precedência:** onde as duas erratas repetem a mesma correção, use a versão de 19nov17. Correções de talents de path, ancestries e spells foram deliberadamente omitidas. A versão de 19nov17 acrescenta também correções posteriores, mas as de spell continuam fora do escopo.

```text
Shadow of the Demon Lord — Movement by Pace table (core p. 37)
The Movement by Pace table should be based on 3 miles per hour: minute 90 yards; hour 3 miles; day 24 miles.

Shadow of the Demon Lord — Crawl (core p. 47)
If prone, you can only move by crawling. You crawl at half your Speed, which can be further reduced by difficult terrain or narrow spaces (to a minimum of 1 yard).

Shadow of the Demon Lord — Weapons table (core p. 103)
Add the finesse property to dart. Add the thrown property to spear under Military Melee Weapons.

Shadow of the Demon Lord — Large animal (core p. 217)
Speed should be 10.

Shadow of the Demon Lord — Flame Genie (core p. 234)
Speed should be 12.

Shadow of the Demon Lord — Giantfall trait (core p. 236)
The giant deals damage equal to 2d6 × its Size to everything in the area where it falls. A creature can make an Agility challenge roll with a number of banes equal to the giant’s Size (minimum 1 bane). On a success, the creature takes half the damage and moves to the nearest open space outside the area. On a failure, the creature becomes trapped under the giant’s body.

Shadow of the Demon Lord — Drain trait (core p. 253)
A living target gains 1 Corruption and takes a –6 penalty to Health that lasts until it completes a rest. While subject to this penalty, the target makes Strength attack rolls and challenge rolls with 1 bane. If the target becomes incapacitated by an attack a shadow makes while the target has this penalty, it dies. At the end of the next round, a new shadow wriggles free from the body and stands up in the nearest open space. The shadow can take the next available turn.

Shadow of the Demon Lord — Lasting Harm trait (core p. 258)
A living target takes a cumulative penalty to Health equal to the damage taken from the attack. If the target becomes incapacitated by an attack a wraith makes while the target has this penalty, it dies. At the end of the next round, a new wraith with half the Health of its creator wriggles free from the body and stands up in the nearest open space. The wraith is compelled for 1 hour by its creator, after which time it can act normally.

Godless — Armored Truck (p. 37)
Increase Health to 80. The armored truck should have an “*” next to its entry.

Godless — ATV (p. 37)
Under Max Speed (a/d), add “; off”.

Godless — Tank (p. 37)
The entry should have “**” and, at the bottom, the second line should lead with “**”.

Godless — Radiation (pp. 52–53), replacement Recovery
Each time a creature suffering from radiation sickness completes a rest, it must make a Strength challenge roll with a number of banes based on its current level of exposure, as shown under Transmission. Results: 20 or higher, move down one stage (minimum stage 0); Success, no change; Failure, move up one stage; 0 or less, move up two stages (maximum stage 4).

Freeport Companion — Atomizer (p. 32), replacement text
An atomizer sprays liquid from its reservoir outward in a fine mist to fill the air inside a cube of space, up to 1 yard on a side, originating from a point you can reach. You must use an action to fill the atomizer with fluid, but, once full, using the atomizer is a minor activity. Although generally used for perfumes, it can spray a single dose of a liquid potion or poison into the area. Any creature in the area must get a success on an Agility challenge roll or be affected by the spray as if it had consumed the potion or poison.

Freeport Companion — Passengers and Occupants (p. 44), replacement paragraph
When a crash occurs, creatures on the object struck and the ship are at risk of injury or falling overboard. On the larger object, 1d20 percent of crew and passengers are lost; on the smaller, 1d20 + 10 percent are lost. If the objects are the same Size, both lose 1d20 + 5 percent. Player characters and important GM-controlled characters/creatures at the points of impact take 3d6 damage on the larger object or 7d6 on the smaller; if the objects are the same Size, creatures on both take 5d6. Affected creatures make Agility challenge rolls: success halves the damage; failure also causes prone; a total of 0 or less also causes the creature to fall overboard.
```


## 88. Auditoria das fontes sem novo bloco autônomo

**Faerie Friends.pdf:** auditado integralmente. O material mecânico é ancestry Lutin, seus starting benefits/equipment e substituições ligadas a paths; por isso não há bloco novo dentro do escopo deste compêndio. [DEPENDÊNCIA OMITIDA]

**Wild Beasts.pdf:** re-auditado nesta rodada. O conteúdo em escopo já estava incorporado na seção 64 (Blooded Warrior, Horned Priest, Horned Champion, Horned Hero e os três Shadow effects); nenhuma duplicata foi criada.

## 89. Checklist de manutenção
Antes de entregar uma versão ampliada deste compêndio, confirme:

- [ ] A nova fonte aparece no manifesto.
- [ ] Regras-base e variantes continuam separadas.
- [ ] Nenhum bloco de ancestry/path foi incluído por acidente.
- [ ] Nenhum bloco completo de spell foi incluído por acidente.
- [ ] Equipamentos mantêm preço/disponibilidade/propriedades quando a fonte os fornece.
- [ ] Criaturas mantêm Difficulty e o restante do stat block.
- [ ] Conflitos/reimpressões são identificados por fonte.
- [ ] As páginas do PDF estão registradas.
- [ ] O arquivo continua pesquisável por nome oficial.

**Versão:** 4.0 — expansão do compêndio para 95 fontes em 2026-09-20; 23 PDFs desta rodada auditados, *Wild Beasts* revalidado sem duplicação e 22 novas fontes registradas no manifesto. A errata de 19nov17 tem precedência sobre a de 10oct17 quando ambas tratam do mesmo ponto.
